subsubtopic: TRIAL OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR IN BRITISH COURT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. Yesterday we learned in a British courtroom, not a Canadian one, that Hugh Hambleton, who is charged with offences under the U.K. Official Secrets Act, was a Soviet spy for more than 30 years in constant touch with Soviet agents, that he had had dinner in a Moscow apartment with the head of the KGB, and that he was found with the most sophisticated Soviet-built espionage equipment in November, 1979.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: TRIAL OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR IN BRITISH COURT
speechtext: In Montreal.

subsubtopic: TRIAL OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR IN BRITISH COURT
speechtext:
This morning in that same courtroom we learned that he had not only turned over to the Soviets thousands of NATO documents but that he turned over 80 of the most top secret documents classified as "Cosmic", to the

November 30, 1982
Ora! Questions
Soviets. In light of the fact that there are thousands of Canadian troops stationed in Germany, has Canada gone out of the business of prosecuting spies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: TRIAL OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR IN BRITISH COURT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is a rhetorical question. Of course, in a proper case where the evidence was there, where the Official Secrets Act would be effective in obtaining a prosecution, there would be a prosecution brought. I would remind my hon. friend that the evidence to which he is referring has been led by the prosecution. There is a case under way now. One assumes that the defence will want to put in evidence as well. I would urge all Hon. Members not to make statements in the House or to characterize evidence in a way which could, if communicated to Great Britain, jeopardize a fair trial. There will be time for discussing matters like this after decisions have been reached by courts in Great Britain.

subsubtopic: TRIAL OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR IN BRITISH COURT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is the Government that will prosecute the Toronto Sun and Peter Worthington, but will not prosecute a true spy.

subsubtopic: TRIAL OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR IN BRITISH COURT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, on May 23, 1980, in this House, in answer to a question directed by the late Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville, the Solicitor General said:
-there is a question as to whether any official secrets at all were obtained to be given to foreign governments. Second, there is a question of whether any of the information that was given, secret or not, was damaging to our country.
That was May, 1980. In light of the statements made by the Attorney General of Great Britain this morning that 80 of the most secret documents which NATO had, were conveyed to the Soviet Union-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: From Canada.
-was the Solicitor General ignorant of those facts when he gave that answer on May 23, or was he just not telling the truth?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am not going to confirm any facts in the matter for now, but I can tell the Hon. Member that I was fully informed about the basis on which the decision was reached by the officials in the Department of Justice and by the law officers of the Crown. As I indicated before, there will be a time when I will be prepared to be more forthcoming about the evidence which we had and the way in which the decision was made, but I urge my hon. friend not to press me to do that now.

Madam Speaker, yesterday in answer to questions that I posed, the Solicitor General said that there was the highest degree of co-operation between the
British authorities and those of our Security Service. I would ask the Solicitor General to confirm reports that appeared for the first time, to my knowledge, in July, 1982, that a Frank Pratt of the Special Services of the RCMP told Mr. Hamble-ton not to go to London or he might be in for "a hostile reception". Is that accurate or is it not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is true that the Security Service had a continuing contact and exchange of information with Mr. Hambleton from the time that the decision was made that there should be no prosecution, and that he was told that if he did go to Great Britain he could meet a hostile reception. But Mr. Hambleton was determined to go, and decided on his own that he would.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Government of the late Mr. Pearson decided that it had sufficient prima facie evidence to strike the Spencer inquiry to look into the activities of a postal employee. The Government also thought it had sufficient prima facie evidence under this Prime Minister to prosecute one Peter Treu. Can the Solicitor General explain to the House why in this case a spy, self-confessed, had been operating for some 30 years, much of that time in Canada, travelling on a Soviet passport, seems to be immune from arrest and prosecution in this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, one of the factors is the difficulties with the Official Secrets Act.
That's nonsense.

My friend has mentioned two cases. I ask him to look at the opinions expressed by the courts about the Official Secrets Act in both of those cases.
The Department of Justice has revisions of the Official Secrets Act under consideration. They have not been brought forward-or were not brought forward-at the time of the Hambleton decision because the McDonald Commission was sitting. It was anticipated that the McDonald Commission might produce recommendations which ought to be taken account of in any amendment or improvement of the Official Secrets Act. That is one of the reasons.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, is the Government conducting any inquiry into the circumstances of this case in order to determine why Hambleton was able to function for as long as he did in this country, and is the Government looking particularly at the Gouzenko files to see whether or not this man was identified at that time? Did the Government receive any information from any other security service, particularly the CIA, identifying Hambleton and, if so, when?
November 30, 1982

I would also like to know when the opinion was given by the Department of Justice that there was insufficient evidence to obtain a conviction, because that is what I take the Solicitor General to mean, not insufficient evidence to support a prosecution, a prima facie case against Hambleton?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the decision was made during the month of January, 1980. The Hon. Member asks if we know a great deal about Hambleton's activities in the country. We do know a great deal about his activities.
As I indicated yesterday outside the House, we learned a great deal more about his activities after the Security Service informed him of the decision reached by the Department of Justice about prosecution. That information was communicated not only to the British but to other friendly intelligence services, one of whom took advantage of the opportunity to come to Canada and interrogate Hambleton further.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who has already referred to Governor Bouey's statement in Toronto yesterday, when he indicated that the Government's Ml policy is not a useful guide to policy. subsubtopic: CHANGE IN MONETARY POLICY GUIDE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Governor has explained extensively the reasons why at the present time he is not going to refer to Ml as the proper criterion. Ml is not a policy. It is a criterion to which the bank refers in its conduct of the monetary policy of the country. There have been significant changes in the banking system which have made the definition of Ml quite inadequate in defining what is actually happening in terms of the currency in circulation and demand deposits. In light of this evolution, which is parallel to a similar evolution in the United States where the Federal Reserve Board has indicated that it is abandoning Ml as a criterion, the bank has come to the conclusion that it should develop broader criteria and refer to the general situation in terms of the exchange rate and the inflation rate as a reference.
As I said, this reference to Ml has been in existence since 1975, but the evolution of the last few months has shown that it is not a useful criterion. The policy remains the same. The policy of the bank is to try to encourage a reduction in the rate of inflation. We have met with considerable success in the last few months in that regard. We hope we will continue to meet with success, and reduce inflation in this country, which will lead to a reduction in interest rates, the creation of more investment and more jobs.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, November 25, consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this Bill has been before us on more than one occasion. There have been interruptions in the debate and therefore 1 think it is worthwhile, as we begin another round on the matter, to recall the import of the Bill.
Those of us who are taking part in the debate no doubt started out by reading Clause 1 of the Bill. In the massive verbiage on the first page we find Clause 1, which reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this section, the amount of the full monthly pension that may be paid to any person for a month in 1983 shall be the lesser of (a) the amount that, but for this subsection, might have been paid for that month-
It goes on, but basically the explanatory note tells us what is the effect of the Bill. We should all recall that the amendment would limit the indexation of the pension to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984 and that it is an amendment to the Bill on Old Age Security.
November 30, 1982

Some facts which are worth recalling at this stage were brought to my attention during the summer recess. I refer to the Times-Colonist of August 28, 1982 in which some interesting extracts from the report of the National Council on Welfare appeared. The article dealt with poverty, which is basically what we are talking about today. People who rely on the old age pension as their only income are in many cases very close to the poverty line. Part of the article indicated that a family of four was poor if it was surviving in a big city on less than $18,243 annually, and that the same family in a rural area was poor with an income below $13,419. Also it indicated that couples in big cities were poor if their income was less than $11,800 and, if they are in rural areas, less than $8,669.
We are talking about poverty, and I think that must be made clear at the outset. The 1980 figures provided by Statistics Canada show that there were 3,475,000 Canadians under the poverty lines. This is a disgraceful situation, and we are talking about reducing the indexation of the incomes of many of these people.
A further piece of information which I think is worth putting on the record appeared in the same article. A CP report from Ottawa indicated that these 3,475,000 poor Canadians represented 15.1 per cent of the total population of Canada. They have been singled out by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to receive less than they would be receiving if the six and five rule were not imposed upon them, as the Bill intends to do.
Further in the article it was indicated that the Council reported that most poor Canadians lived on incomes which were hundreds and often thousands of dollars below the poverty lines. Also it indicated that 80 per cent of poor families are 10 per cent to 20 per cent below the poverty lines and that 75 per cent of poor single persons are more than 20 per cent under the poverty lines.
One of the reasons people are in this dreadful situation is inflation, which is a component part of the debate. The Minister is intending, for those people who are old and on pensions, that we should ignore inflation and impose upon them the six and five formula which would provide them with increases in their income well below the inflation rate.
My final reference to the article is this. It indicated that incomes have been eroded by an inflation rate of 12.5 per cent in 1981 and will be eroded by 11.5 per cent in 1982. We now have the context in which the debate is now being set.
There is a scheme afoot in the Bill to impose upon those with fixed incomes increases of no more than 6 per cent in 1983 and no more than 5 per cent in 1984, while I am afraid we can bet our bottom dollar that the inflation rates will be three and four points higher than that for each of those years.
We are being asked to agree in Parliament to offering those on old age pensions to accept less than the inflation rate. I think this is absolutely disgusting. Also it explains why not one Liberal, aside from the Minister, has stood up to defend the Bill. The Minister alone has had the nerve to rise and suggest the imposition of this iniquitous six and five formula on pensioners. Obviously the Liberals are staying away in droves
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
and are counting on their overwhelming majority to do the trick for them, to impose on their mothers and grandmothers, those who gave them the opportunity to get to this place, the six and five formula. It is a disgraceful performance if ever 1 saw one.
Some of us on regular incomes and still in the work force can afford the six and five formula. There are promotion prospects for some, but pensioners are on fixed incomes with little prospect of bettering them. There are limits if they receive too much in the way of incidental income. They lose one part or the other of that income. It will be a great deal tougher for them.
It is worth looking at some other facts or trends in the aging of our population to indicate how the problem will be aggravated in terms of numbers. I hope it is not for this reason that this shoddy Government is hoping to save money, but the population of Canada is aging. There are almost 700,000 fewer Canadians under the age of 20 than there were ten years ago, but there are 800,000 Canadians over the age of 60. That is the group which the Government is attacking. If we want to project even further into the next century, it is estimated that by the year 2020 there will be only two or three workers in Canada to support every non-worker. These are the ones who will have to pay the taxes to provide assistance for those who have retired from the work force.
Is this the reason the Government is trying to save money today, in order to look after those people 40 years down the line? I wonder if this also has something to do with those public servants who manage to arrange for themselves a posting to Paris to live on $170,000 a year, or those who manage to arrange to be sent to the French Riviera to learn French at almost as iniquitous a sum? These disgraceful misplacements of priorities, these iniquitously, wasteful public expenditures, make it more difficult, I would have thought, to defend a Bill of this sort. It certainly must have a bearing on the attitudes of those on the other side of the House who are afraid to stand up and say something, although 1 see some of them are making notes. I hope they will stand up when the time comes to defend. I would rather see them fight the proposal that is made by their Minister. I wonder whether there is a single one of them who has the courage to do that.
I think it is worth looking at poverty levels. I have been looking at them and we have been talking about poverty levels. In essence, we have been dealing with poverty levels at this time because the Government is thinking of imposing-I will not be a party to it-on those who are within the poverty range its six and five formula. But what about out there in the harsh world? The inflation rate from one year to the next will go up. I suspect it will be 9 per cent or 10 per cent next year. I do not think, and I am sure there is no one on the Government side who in his right mind believes, that the six and five formula will bring the inflation rate down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the next two years, especially when this formula is going to

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
be imposed on those who cannot afford it. With inflation stalled at 11 per cent or 12 per cent-maybe even 10 per cent-the 6 per cent imposition will hurt. Do you know whom it is going to hurt, Mr. Speaker? It will hurt our parents, our grandparents and our uncles, those who have provided a good life for us. Those are the people who will be hurt, and this is the Government that will follow the leader and try to impose this formula on that segment of the population.
I think it is worth putting a few figures on the record. I am going to deal with couples. I could deal with a family of four, but by the time people have reached retirement age it is normally a couple-hopefully a couple and not just a single person, lonesome, by himself-a couple who have reached the age when they are relying on the Old Age Security payments. The OAS payment for two, according to current levels, is $246.92. This would produce a grand total of $5,924 in a year. In addition, if that were their only income, they could perhaps draw on the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which would give them another $4,587; together with the $5,924 that would give a couple a total of $10,511. Let me repeat that figure: a couple would get a total of $10,511. The poverty level has been variously calculated by a variety of institutions, the principal of which is the Senate report on poverty.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, and that of those who are planning to vote for this Bill to a recent publication which came to me on November 8, compliments of the Senator in charge of the Committee on Poverty. The poverty lines in 1981, according to the Senate committee poverty line criteria, amounted to $12,300. According to the StatsCan revised low-income cut-off, the amount is much lower, but let us take the higher figure of $12,300 as the poverty level. If your annual income is below that figure, you are in want. I think that is what poverty means. In 1981 if you received $12,300, you were in need.
I think it is also worth drawing to the attention of Hon. Members that in 1971 the poverty line stood at $4,040. If we put those figures side by side, we will find that between 1971 and 1981 the poverty level has trebled. Inflation has managed to triple the poverty line. The level at which people are in dire need is an amount of $12,300 today. What about the figure I have just quoted, the maximum that two people both drawing Old Age Security and the GIS can get, of $10,500? There is a difference there of some $2,200, which gives a percentage variance between what they are drawing and where the poverty line is of 11 per cent, the percentage of inflation. These are the people on your right-hand side, Mr. Speaker, who propose to impose the six and five formula over the next two years upon those who will be $2,200 below the poverty level.
How is that trend of tripling inflation in ten years to be contained for those on fixed incomes? The six and five formula will not do it. The six and five formula will not do it for those on fixed incomes at all. There will be pressures elsewhere on society to inflate-to ask for more-because of the inflationary factor that I have suggested will be 10 per cent and 11 per cent.
Furthermore, savings have been discouraged by this Government by making fulsome and false promises which are now being somewhat hedged. There was an indication that the just society-just for the Liberals, I suppose-of "Don't worry, we will look after you" will have to be reneged. The Liberals will have to qualify that promise.
Investment has been discouraged by this Government over the years by interfering unduly in the marketplace. Let us see where that interference has taken place. For example, Pacific Petroleums was acquired not because there were resources and futures in the ground, but because it gave a storefront image to the Government. Merit in British Columbia was also an outlet for refined products. To my recollection, Petrofina will cost $1.5 billion without producing one single drop of new oil, let alone a barrel, just to provide another storefront in eastern Canada for Petro-Canada. We were recently told that it would cost approximately $300 million to acquire BP Canada. That original figure has now risen to almost $600 million.
This total amount gives us an indication of where the Government's priorities lie. They do not lie with those who have provided us with what we have today. They are the people who are being affected by this proposal today through the six and five formula. They are less able to shield themselves from its effects than the rest of us are.
I have spoken in the House previously about the current consumer price index. I have suggested previously and I will suggest again that there should be a new index for those to whom the old index does not really apply. I would like to go through this index and explain which areas I believe are completely unsuitable to those it is being applied to.
For example, food is supposed to be responsible for 21.5 per cent of the total index. Consumption of food at home represents 16.8 per cent and meals away from home represent 4.6 per cent. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, how many pensioners are able to spend a quarter of their food money at restaurants? I suggest that there are very few and, in fact, probably none. That figure makes a distortion of this aspect of the consumer price index.
Housing is supposed to represent 34 per cent of the index. The breakdown of that figure is 19 per cent for shelter, 8.6 per cent for operations and 6.4 per cent for furnishings. I wonder whether that percentage for furnishings, which is approximately 20 per cent, is really needed by old age pensioners or could even be purchased by them. They have spent their lives accumulating their treasures and their tables and chairs and other furnishings; they do not need to spend that amount of money on furnishings. Once again this is a distortion of the housing portion of the index.
Clothing represents 10 per cent of the disposable income. This percentage is then broken down among men's clothing, women's clothing, girls' and boys' clothing, infant clothing and other clothing materials and related services. This portion could probably stay in its present form.
November 30, 1982

Another segment of the CPI concerns transportation. It represents almost 16 per cent, 14 per cent of which relates to privately-owned transportation. How many of the people with whom we are concerned today-those who are living 10 per cent below the poverty line now-can afford private transportation? Only 2 per cent in this index is attributable to public transportation. Nearly all the old age pensioners I know use public transportation because they cannot afford to drive their own cars.
Only 4 per cent of the CPI is attributable to health and personal care. A greater percentage is likely needed in this area for those in this particular age bracket. I suggest there is a distortion in this area as well which should be corrected.
This distortion is evident when we see that 8 per cent of the CPI is for recreation, reading and education. That is twice as much as health care. I think the breakdown on recreation, reading and education is worth putting on the record. Of that 8.3 per cent for this item, 6.6 per cent is for recreation. What does this recreation involve? Skiing or the purchase of ski equipment? Is 6 per cent of that 8 per cent recreation for people over the age of 65? Let us be serious. This is an index that is not prepared or applicable to those old age pensioners. Reading represents 1.7 per cent of that 8 per cent. I suggest that this figure is probably higher, while a great deal of reading material, of course, comes from public libraries. Tobacco is almost 2 per cent; I hope that percentage is dropping. With respect to alcohol, how many pensioners can afford to spend 4.3 per cent of their disposable income for recreation, reading and education purposes on alcohol? That is one-half of what the amount attributed to reading, recreation and education.
Therefore, I suggest that a separate index for the elderly is required which is properly geared to the purchasing patterns of those who are in this particular age bracket. This is the type of index which should apply to the increments in the Old Age Security and to the GIS.
The whole concept that a consumer price index can be applied universally across the country is a matter of folly. Therefore, I speak up for these pensioners because they are defenceless, both financially and economically. I also speak up for them because they are our mothers and fathers and in some cases our grandmothers and grandfathers. They gave us this country and the benefits we enjoy. Why is the Government planning in this legislation to rob them of the benefits they gave us to enjoy and which they should be able to enjoy themselves in their declining years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be taking part in the debate on Bill C-131, which, Hon. Members will recall, is part of our anti-inflation measures. First of all, I have been wondering why Members of the Progressive Conservative Party were opposed to a Bill that placed restrictions on increases in old age security benefits for persons who were
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
relatively well-off. We must remember that the Canadian government has maintained full indexation for all senior citizens receiving the income supplement and has also agreed to indexation of the basic amount for this group. I wondered why so many Members of the Progressive Conservative Party were opposed to a 6 and 5 per cent ceiling on indexation, a measure senior citizens are being asked to accept as part of the fight against inflation. While listening to the previous speaker,
I asked my colleague how old the Hon. Member was. In fact, he is getting his old age security pension, and I now understand why the Members of the Progressive Conservative Party are not standing up for needy senior citizens and are taking up the cause of senior citizens with big pensions to keep them from being affected.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members on the Progressive Conservative side should be honest with themselves. During the short time they were in power, they were ready to throw out universality of pension benefits. In fact, it was worse than that, and I feel that this House cannot afford to be hypocritical and play politics with a subject of this magnitude.
Mr. Speaker, when I realized that Hon. Members on the Progressive Conservative side were defending their own interests in connection with Old Age Security benefits, I decided that I would not give their arguments further consideration. Mr. Speaker, unlike Hon. Members on the Progressive Conservative side, this summer Members from Quebec worked instead of going on trips. I chaired a committee which included a number of my colleagues, a committee which met with senior citizens groups throughout Quebec to discuss inflation and the 6 and 5 policy, and any other subjects that were of interest to them.
Mr. Speaker, the Members of the committee were: Senator Yvette Rousseau, the Hon. Member for Verdun (Mr. Savard), the Hon. Member for Missisquoi (Mr. Bachand), the Hon. Member for Saint-Michel (Mrs. Killens) and the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Dion). Mr. Speaker, while all our colleagues on the Progressive Conservative side were probably travelling around Europe, we were working and truly defending the cause of our senior citizens. The groups we met included the Senior Citizens' Forum, the AQDR, the FADOQ and also members of senior citizens' clubs and individual senior citizens, the real people and not senior citizens who sit in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, at these meetings we explained what the Government of Canada was doing for senior citizens. Both Progressive Conservative and New Democratic Party Members have told us only about incomes, and I may remind Hon. Members-since the Progressive Conservatives failed to mention this, either on purpose or because they forgot or

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
because they are not aware of the program-that the Canadian Government is maintaining full indexation for senior citizens receiving the income supplement. This supplement is fully indexed to the cost of living and the same applies to the basic pension paid to individuals who are eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is also important to remember all the other programs that are geared to senior citizens-programs that are concerned with income, housing, health, recreation, cultural activities and home care. I think all Hon. Members are aware of the Canadian Government's basic pension, Guaranteed Income Supplement and Spouse's allowance programs, which are three of the most important programs to which all Canadians have access in connection with Old Age Security benefits. There is also the Canada Pension Plan, and for Quebecers, the Quebec Pension Plan. As for housing, it is unfortunate but among the people we met, I am sure that many were not aware of all the programs the Canadian Government is financing, either alone or jointly with provincial or municipal Governments. First of all, we have what is known in Quebec as low rental housing. In this area, the Canadian Government finances 50 per cent of the operating deficit for subsidized housing, and in Quebec, it is probably true that between 50 and 56 per cent of such housing is occupied by senior citizens, who are thus able to pay lower rents than they would do otherwise. Another program wholly financed by the Canadian Government-here again, there is a high percentage of senior citizens, is Co-operative and Non-Profit Housing. The program is 100 per cent financed by the Canadian Government and is allowed an annual subsidy in order to maintain interest rates at 2 per cent for 35 years, and on top of that, there are start-up fund grants for groups, which operate autonomously.
There is also another area, which provincial governments prefer not to mention, and which also falls under housing. I am referring to senior citizens' homes, which are extremely important for this age group. The housing units set aside by the Canadian Government under Section 56.1 for 2 per cent financing are very often used by the Province of Quebec-I must say I am more knowledgeable about the situation in this particular Province-for senior citizens' homes. Unfortunately, the Province of Quebec, and I suppose the same applies to other provincial governments, does not mention the Canadian Government's contribution in financing these homes.

Mr. Speaker, another area that is very important to senior citizens is health care, and everybody is aware that 50 per cent of the cost of operating Local Community Service Centres or other health care services is paid by the Government.
Another area is that of home care services for senior citizens. In addition, we have recreational and other activities for senior citizens. As far as home care services are concerned, I
mentioned earlier in this connection the Department of National Health and Welfare and the financing of Local Community Service Centres which provide home care services. Most ridings also seem to have community development programs or summer employment projects. These projects are used by groups to create jobs and also to provide home care services for senior citizens. I know that in my riding, since I became a Member, the first two or three projects that are approved usually have been home care service projects for senior citizens.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, every riding, every parish and every village has its senior citizens' dub. Before, senior citizens had to stay home and twiddle their thumbs. Now they have activities that are geared to their needs and especially designed for them, and this has been happening all across Canada, in every village, city and municipality, thanks to the New Horizons Program. Senior citizens groups themselves define their own programs, and the Department of National Health and Welfare, and its extremely efficient minister, are responding to the needs of these people.
Mr. Speaker, with the Quebec Caucus Committee on Senior Citizens, I would like to offer a few conclusions, since my Progressive Conservative colleague held a meeting of all Progressive Conservative Members aged 65 or over to find out whether they would go along with the 6 per cent ceiling on indexation or preferred full indexation. First of all, we received a press release:
The Forum of Senior Citizens and the pension program
-a press release issued by this group after their meeting with the Quebec caucus members, and I quote:
The Forum of Senior Citizens of Montreal is pleased with the anti-inflationary measures recommended by the Federal Government, and it has agreed to accept the indexing of the basic pension under the old age security program at 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984.
Mr. Speaker, this is a group which truly represents the real needs of senior citizens in the Montreal area.
We also have an article from a newspaper in the riding of my colleague from Missisquoi (Mr. Bachand), which reports the conclusions of the meeting, and I quote:
Another program was approved outright by the people at the meeting, namely, the 6 and 5 program-
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that the Members from Quebec are not afraid to take a stand, but we are not about to stand up for the same interests as the Progressive Conservative Party. Fortunately, not all Members of the Progressive Conservative Party are defending only the interests of the very rich, but in any case, we are here to protect the interests of senior citizens, of people who are indigent. These are the people we met, and they supported us in our intention to vote for this Bill, because these people know perfectly well that the fight against inflation is going to help them. We have a very good example of this in the area of subsidized housing. Even if
November 30, 1982

we did maintain full indexing of pensions, the Government of Quebec, through its Minister of Housing, Mr. Tardif, has announced that the rates for all subsidized housing in Quebec would be increased by between 20 and 30 per cent. So of course, senior citizens preferred to take our side, not so much because they approved limited indexation but in order to convince the Government of Quebec and the other provincial governments and the private sector that they would have to do their part to bring inflation down to six per cent.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I wish to congratulate the Minister for the work she has done in the health sector in general and for what she has done for senior citizens. I can assure you that I shall be proud to vote in favour of this Bill and thus help those who need it most.

There has been a full two days' debate in this House. It was begun by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) putting forward her proposals. As she put them forward I watched her face, and I thought that if ever I saw a Minister not convinced about the righteousness of her brief, a brief which attacked the senior citizens of the country, that she on platform after platform had said she would defend, it was on that day in the House.

speechtext: Where is it?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
An indication of just how bad the atmosphere is in the Government Party is that today, well into the debate, is the first time there has been a private Liberal Member of Parliament rise to make a short speech extolling the virtue of attacking the senior citizens of the country, those people who receive Old Age Security in Canada. These people are more exposed in terms of inflation and uncertainty than any other group.
The Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) is behind the curtain nodding his head and saying it is not true. I want to say to the Member from Ottawa Centre, come into the House, go to your place and defend this attack on the senior citizens of the country. At the same time defend the attack of your Government on the public servants of the country, on the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, on those who served the country as members of the Armed Forces, and their widows and families. State the position. Do not stand behind the curtain; come into the House and state the position. Are they going to stand with those pieces of legislation, or are they going to vote against them? I have heard people say they are against this Bill as it is written; they are against another
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Bill as it is written. I want to know when the votes are counted where they stand.
I want to say to my friends, those who have remained silent over there on Old Age Security, that there is a power in a Government caucus if a Government caucus is prepared to exercise it. This seems to be the only Parliament in the western world where all of the discussions take place in private. I was in the United Kingdom a week ago yesterday and watched a debate and finally a vote in their House of Commons, where the Conservative Government of Great Britain was attacking a socialist program. I listened to Conservative Member after Member after Member of the Parliament in Great Britain stand up and attack the proposal by the Government. When the time came they did not scuttle into their seats to vote confidence in the Government; they abstained, and one of them even voted against the Government.
That is how Government listen. I and my other friends make speeches in this House of Commons but no one on that side listens. Those members of the Treasury benches will not listen. That is the way the system works. We can state a certain position. The Government will be accountable at the next election.
If there is real opposition to something, whether with respect to pensions for Old age Security recipients or with respect to public servants, members of the RCMP, the Armed Services, their widows or their families, and if there is an honest belief that what the Government is doing is wrong, then it is morally wrong for Members of Parliament not to stand up and vote against, or abstain, but never to use the excuse that confidence in the Government is at stake, that the Government may fall if they exercise their right of independence. Yet that is what they are saying. I say that is wrong. There is not a self-respecting person in the country who thinks about the system who does not believe that that is wrong.
The situation is this. If the Government of Canada was defeated on Bill C-133 or defeated on this Bill involving Old Age Security-of course, it is an important Bill-I will wager that they would not dare face the country on their attack on senior citizens. You bet they would not, Mr. Speaker. The next day they would be in here with a motion of confidence. That is when the Liberal Members and others who have confidence in the Liberal Government would have the chance to vote confidence. But not with respect to a piece of legislation; that is not how the system works.
The Pearson precedent has certainly affected the question of confidence in the Canadian House of Commons, but it does not only affect those who are against the Government because of where we sit in the House or because of how we feel; it also affects those who support the Government.
I want to say to my friend from Ottawa Centre and to all my friends opposite, whether we are dealing with this Bill C-131 or Bill C-133 with respect to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act for the broad Public Service of the country, that there is an opportunity for them to stand up and defeat their Government on the Bill. I will wager them dollars to donuts that the next day they will have a chance to stand up

Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
and support their Government in terms of confidence. That is the essence of the Pearson precedent in 1968.
When I read stories about certain Members of Parliament changing their ground just a wee bit, I have to ask myself, why? Who is so mesmerized by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he says it is a matter of confidence? If it is a matter of confidence, I wonder how some of those Members would appreciate going to the country on the basis of attacking senior citizens-which is how it will be construed-or attacking those Pensioners under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. That is the raw politics of it.
It goes beyond raw politics in this Bill. I hold it as a principle that those who are outside the work force, those who are making no contribution in the real sense in terms of work, in terms of making demands, those who have run their course in terms of a regular work day and ask nothing else but that they have a chance to live in a reasonable amount of peace, ought not to be the tools or the levers for Government redistribution of income. It is as simple as that.
We brought in indexing and all of us supported indexing. Why? Because we said those people were different, they do not have the levers to bargaining power that others have. They need to be protected. Whether it be a new index, a senior citizens' index, the consumer price index or whatever it is, we must protect them. It is no protection, in my judgment, for that group to see their indexing limited.
The Public Service accepts that the indexing of their wages and salaries should be limited. They do not like it. Members of Parliament do not like it when it happens to them, but they accept it. Why? Because they can bargain again and hopefully make it up. But the problem is that those people in the latter years of their life cannot do so. You just do not lose those two years; you lose the progression upwards with the index whenever it is taken off.
If the Government will not forecast anything in the economy in terms that are reliable because they say it is impossible, how can they say with certainty today that inflation will be reduced to six and five? I hope it will be, but how can they say that? Why should they leave those people exposed?
That is the issue of principle, pure and simple. It is not just a little matter of administration, shifting funds from here to there. Whether talking about this bill, Old Age Security, or about the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, there is a contract, an agreement and an understanding.
This Bill goes right to the heart of social programs. It is the basis of it. There is much more than just an agreement or contract; there is a moral obligation on society. It is becoming apparent that that moral obligation is getting greater every year. The statistics are startling. I will not trouble the House with them because I understand another Member wants to follow me and I will listen to her. However, the statistics in terms of the aging and our obligation are growing.
November 30, 1982
They are growing in a time when we have decided to undercut the elderly in terms of our obligation. That is wrong. Therefore, I intend to vote against the Bill. No amount of petty-fogging, no amount of meetings with groups of senior citizens in Quebec and no amount of meetings of any kind will stop me from doing that.
I do not say this because senior citizens in my constituency have been in touch with me. Long before I saw this Bill, I held it to be morally wrong. It is morally wrong for this Parliament to support that proposition. Parliament has a special obligation to senior citizens. They look to us to answer that special obligation. They look to this Minister to answer that special obligation. I do not know what they are saying in Quebec to the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie, but they are saying something different to the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton and, I dare say, to other Members of this House.
The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie said that when we, Members of Parliament, were travelling in Europe they, the great Liberal Party, were defending the Old Age Security payment. Some defence! A couple of days of debate, one Minister and one Member getting up to defend it, not on the basis of this program but on the basis of other programs the Government has put in place. We agree with those other programs. There is no argument there. The argument with this Bill is solely and simply whether it is right to cap that index in terms of recipients of the Old Age Security.
If that index was put there to ensure that those who are defenceless are defended, in the sense that we in Parliament on both sides of the House defend them, then indexing had a purpose. We ought not to forget the purpose. Those who are defenceless look to us to protect their standard of living. This is not going to be done willy-nilly in the dark of night in a budget speech of which there was no advance warning. We voted against that budget speech which contained exactly this provision.
I want Members opposite to go to their senior citizens and then get up in this House, every one of them, and tell the country that they are supporting denying full benefits to the senior citizens of this country. I do not want them to sit there silently but to get up and speak. There must be someone opposite who agrees with me. I cannot believe that the Liberal Party is so bereft of the principle it once stood for; I cannot believe that is the case.
I want those opposite to go to the Government House Leader and ask him to remove their gags so that they can get up to speak on this very important Bill. This Bill is going to be fought in the House of Commons for as long as we can fight it, using every legitimate parliamentary means. When it goes to committee, and I assume it will at some time if the Government is so determined, we will fight it there.
I say to my friends opposite that it is quite safe for them to vote against a Bill involving changes in Old Age Security. It is quite safe to vote against a Bill to change the arrangements with respect to supplementary retirement benefits. The Government will not be defeated. Does anyone think the Government would go to the country standing behind in the polls as it
November 30, 1982

is at present? Can anyone imagine going to the country on the backs of the senior citizens of Canada? I would lay dollars to doughnuts that sitting in the Government House Leader's file already is the motion of confidence that would be brought in the next day. Therefore, you can all support your Party and support your Government-and I must say I have a prejudiced view-with all its supposed strengths, but still take a stand in terms of the senior citizens of this country.
I want some Members opposite, not just one, to stand up and say they have had enough of this. That is the essence of Parliament. The Canadian Parliament is light years behind the British Parliament in terms of how it deals with matters of confidence. Every time I go overseas, I never cease to be amazed at the courage of backbenchers, whether Liberal, Labour or Conservative, and I assume members of the new party whom I have not seen in action. Their independence is amazing. The first question asked by the Prime Minister of Great Britain or the Leader of the Government is: "Will the caucus stand for this; what will the caucus say?" That is the last question asked in Canada.
This is a chance for my friends on the other side. I will ask them to do this only one more time this session, when we deal with Bill C-133, the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. It is one chance for them to stand up for a principle that there is a special obligation owed by the Government and Parliament as well as the people of Canada to whose who are no longer part of the work force and cannot defend themselves through unions and other things. I will ask them one more time to stand up and be counted on the side of what is morally right in terms of the people whom this Government and this Parliament pledged to serve.
I thank the House for its attention. I congratulate the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie for rising to his feet to defend the indefensible with the eloquence of the condemned. In the event of a vote against the senior citizens of this country, those who vote had better know that they are going to be watched by a growing constituency in Canada.
