speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as this is my first speech in the House I would like to take the opportunity to pay tribute to my immediate predecessors who served here with distinction; John Gilbert, now His Honour Judge Gilbert, and Bob Rae, now the Member for York South in the Ontario legislature who is seeking to end 40-odd years of Tory rule in Ontario and establish the first Social Democratic Government in Ontario.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Another of my illustrious predecessors is still a Member of this House, the Hon. Member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees). I am sorry he is not in the House at the moment. He said he would be out looking for a fist fight in the corridor, and if he could make it back he would be back for his honourable mention! I share with these gentlemen the
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
honour of representing a very fine riding, Broadview-Greenwood, and 1 am deeply grateful to the citizens of that riding for having elected me in one of the more colourful, interesting and stormy by-elections in recent years on October 12.
I have chosen to make my first speech on pensions because this is a matter of utmost importance and one on which I have personally done a lot of work, both as an activist in the women's movement, a founding member of the Ontario Committee on the Status of Women, as president of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, and as a member of the Ontario NDP Women's Committee. I regret that I am joining this debate not on a matter of pension reform but on cutbacks. Reforms are what we surely need, and Bill C-131 is one of the nastiest, stingiest and meanest pieces of Liberal legislation to come before this House.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It takes money away from our pensioner population, for the most part people on low, fixed incomes, the people least able to bear the load. It is unfair in the extreme and is aimed at people who have worked and raised families, survived the depression of the 1930s and lived through difficult economic times before there was unemployment insurance. It is aimed at people who have low private pensions, if any, a great number of them, especially women, with no private pensions at all or the least possible under the Canada Pension Plan.
I want also to protest the hypocritical way in which this legislation has been introduced. The principle of the Minister of Finance's (Mr. Lalonde's) economic statement was not to "abandon the victims of the recession", not to "put the axe" to the social security system which has been decades in the making. I know pension reform has been a Government concern over the past few years. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has called it the highest social policy priority of the Government. A national pensions conference was held in 1981 at which women's organizations, among others, participated and where reform was the agenda. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself has spoken on the issue, I recall in the election of 1979, specifically dealing with ways to improve pensions for women. I even went to a Liberal Party function to hear the address, which will show my great devotion to duty in this respect. Then what happened? Instead of reform we have cutbacks. The Minister of National Health and Welfare even has the gall to present this legislation as an invitation to voluntary heroism and self-sacrifice for the national good. I quote from her speech of November 18:
We are asking 1.1 million old age pensioners to help lead the way in the fight against inflation. I am very conscious of the sacrifice we are asking of them.
I have to stress that it is not without reluctance that we make this request.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a very devious way to refer to a Bill which in fact has nothing voluntary about it at all. If the Minister meant what she said, she would send out a letter to the pensioners concerned and ask them if they would like to lead the way in fighting inflation. They would have the option of sending a little card back saying they wanted to have their pension cheque cut in order to fight inflation to the ground. If

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
they were not willing to engage in this heroic action, then their pensions cheques would be indexed fully as they would otherwise be without this legislation. That surely would be the honest way if it were truly a voluntary program.
Let us consider for a moment how this sorry state of affairs has arisen. We all know the Minister is not in fact a monster who takes pleasure in making pensioners live on less money. She is under pressure as a result of the Government's woeful mismanagement of the economy.
With regard to unemployment and falling tax revenues, the Government's job is clearly difficult. It cannot rely, as it has in the past, on selling off our resources because in a world recession the demand for these resources naturally falls too. An adequate income security system requires a healthy economy to support it and that is precisely what we do not have in Canada. That is why my Party is continuing to stress the strategic problems of our economy and the need for major reform through an industrial strategy. But in the meantime, without substantial economic reform, there are alternatives.
By the Minister's own estimate 1.1 million pensioners will lose $55 each in 1983, which would save the Government $61.5 million. That happens to be approximately the cost of Government advertising in one year. We could cut out the entire Government advertising budget, save the money, and it would spare us a great deal of propaganda.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is only half the cost.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That money is a drop in the bucket in terms of corporate give-aways and military expenditures, which the Government still plans to increase. It is the kind of money which can be made up merely by cutting luxuries like foreign embassies and other unnecessary expenditures. The NDP has been scrutinizing Government expenditures for moneys to divert for job-creation programs. We have come up with far greater success than the savings from these Old Age Security cutbacks.
Clearly with a modest effort the Government could come up with a more equitable way of finding the money. This is a sort of no-win situation. If inflation is really only 6 per cent or less, clearly we do not need the Bill at all. If inflation is around 6 per cent or a little bit higher, it is not going to save very much money, so why bother? But if inflation is really substantial, then the Bill is unconscionable. So in all three cases, we really do not need it.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
We in the NDP feel particularly strong about pension cutbacks because it was our party and our predecessors who fought for a public pension system in the first place. A few points in this history are well worth noting because they are still relevant today. It was back in 1925 that we had the first success in establishing public pensions, long after a number of western European countries instituted them. It was then a minority Government situation. J. S. Woods-worth and A. A. Heaps, as labour representatives-because this was before the CCF was formed-made a pensions Bill a
condition of their support. They offered to support either the Liberals or the Conservatives, whichever would bring in a public pension Bill. The Conservatives said no, the Liberals said yes. A Bill was duly passed but then turned down by the Senate.
Perhaps there is a lesson to be learned here because the Conservatives suffered a serious defeat in the next election. After that election the Bill was reintroduced, passed in the House and then the Senate, and thus Canada got its first public pension for persons 70 years and over, based on a means test, and it was $20 a month.
Expanding and increasing the old age pension has continued to be a priority of the CCF and NDP. Universal Old Age Security at $40 a month was achieved in 1951. Indexing began in 1966, and full indexing in 1972. But note that the only increase in real terms-that is, beyond inflation-took place in 1973 when again we were in a minority Government situation and again it was pressure from the NDP which got this real increase. The sad fact is that the amount of the Old Age Security has remained low. When introduced in 1951, it was 17 per cent of the average industrial wage, and has now fallen to about 14 per cent. Now the NDP is urging reinstatement to the level it was back in that very regressive decade of the 1950s. This is scarcely a radical demand.
Even with the Guaranteed Income Supplement, Mr. Speaker, the income of elderly couples hovers only around the poverty line, and for the single elderly, mainly women, the amount falls below. It is women who are mainly dependent on public, non-contributory pensions, for it is they who have spent most of their lives caring for children and there is no pension for doing that most important work.
As a new Member of the House I am proud of the role my predecessors in the CCF and the NDP have played in pension reform. I am proud to be in the caucus with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has been the most vigorous and successful fighter for public pensions in this country.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Pension reform is a subject on which I promise to be very active myself. I am glad to see the Conservatives now joining us in fighting the Government on Bill C-131, but I regret to say that it is a little bit too late.
We have heard stirring speeches, notably from the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), but where were the Conservatives when we needed them last summer when the Government introduced six and five? Alas, the Conservatives voted for six and five then. They are making speeches now so that they can tell their voters, especially their senior voters, that they opposed the Old Age Security cutbacks. But they did not oppose the Bill and the principle when it really mattered. It was the New Democratic Party that fought alone last summer when the Tories, with their superior
November 30, 1982

numbers, could have stopped the Government. Instead, they shamefully supported it.
Finally, let me point out that there is still much that can be done for pension reform, even with the present constraints. We could, for example, act immediately to improve contributory public pensions. The Canada Pension Plan is an excellent plan in universality and portability. Its main defect is that the pension is too low. Our object is to raise the CPP to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage. This is a long-term ambition, but we could at least begin the process now.
Another important reform is to include homemakers in the CPP, at least by instituting the drop-out provision. It is true that Ontario vetoed this measure, but Ontario has since had a Royal Commission on Pensions that recommended accepting it. When have the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare last spoken to Premier Davis about this? Surely now is the time to put pressure on Ontario to move.
Next, we could improve private pensions with regard to portability, vesting, survivors' benefits and the splitting of pension credits on marriage dissolution. We could end discrimination by sex in annuities. We know what is wrong with private pensions and it will not require public expenditure to put that right because these are contributory pensions. What is required is legislation, regulation and co-ordination with the Provinces. Surely this is an important enough matter to give it really high priority.
In closing, let me return to the immediate question of Bill C-131. The answer must be no, no, no! Whatever our economic problems, taking it out on the elderly on fixed incomes at the poverty line is not an acceptable solution in a decent society. If the Government cannot be progressive, imaginative, creative, or competent, let it at least be decent. I ask the Government to withdraw Bill C-131.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I do not agree with all the comments of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), I want to congratulate her on the excellent maiden speech she just delivered to the House.
I welcome the opportunity to speak today on Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, because I am deeply concerned about the welfare of our senior citizens and particularly the 11,000 who live in my riding of Leeds-Grenville. This legislation, introduced into this House by the Government of Canada, is going to add an undue measure of hardship to a sector of our community that cannot even begin to find the resources with which to cope.
This morning I attended a public forum organized by the Ontario Advisory Council on Senior Citizens. The chairman, Frances McHale, had the pleasure of going to Vienna to attend the United Nations World Assembly on Aging and did a lot of work at that Assembly. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer), was also a member of that delegation. In Brockville today the forum is
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
discussing the problems faced by senior citizens. I think it is very apropos that we, too, discuss this matter today.
In the few weeks that I have been a Member of Parliament I have received a great number of representations from senior citizens in my riding. They are concerned about the effect this legislation will have on their day-to-day lives. They are becoming increasingly troubled about falling further and further behind in their never-ending battle to keep up with inflation.
The majority of senior citizens in Leeds-Grenville and indeed the majority of single pensioners have had to resort to living in senior citizens' housing because they could no longer afford the constantly increasing expense of owning and operating their own homes-homes in which they have rich and fond memories of growing up and homes to which they returned after marriage to raise their families.
We have a tremendous number of beautiful old homesteads all over Leeds-Grenville and I am appalled at the great number that are up for sale, the great number that have been converted into multiple dwellings because the elderly who lived in them for the past 60 years or so can no longer afford to pay a heating bill that runs into hundreds and hundreds of dollars per year, or the hydro bill, or the cost of putting gasoline in their car to drive back and forth to town to see the family doctor, or buy the groceries needed to sustain themselves. These people do not want to give up their homes, but they have been put into a position of having to do so because the economy of this country is in such a tragic state.
The alternative is being forced to move into senior citizen housing where they have a room or a suite with a common recreation area. Certainly this accommodation is adequate but the choice, the freedom of choosing, is an option that has been taken away from them. Surely this is not what they deserve for having devoted their lives to raising the future citizens of this country.
I have spent many afternoons talking to senior citizens in Leeds-Grenville, visiting them in their apartments, rooms and homes. They tell me time and time again that they do not want to be put out to pasture like tired and faithful old horses. They tell me they want to remain productive and useful. They want to remain an important part of our society, a society they were instrumental in building. But without the necessary income, our senior citizens will not be able to continue participating in the activities of the community.
In my riding, and I know this is the case throughout the rest of the country, the elderly try to be active year round with outings on bus trips, seminars and social events. I would hate to see them have to curtail their activities simply because they no longer have that extra dollar or two to spend on these so-called luxuries. These people have knowledge and wisdom to offer us, gained through years of experience, and they should have the opportunity to do so. Instead, they are forced to sit at home and waste away. They should be able to grow old with dignity, not with despair.
In the past, the old age pension had been indexed to the rising cost of living in an attempt to enable pensioners to keep

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
pace with the increasing cost of day-to-day expenses. On November 18, in an answer to a question asked by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, as reported at page 20773 of Hansard:
The Hon. Member talks of protection against inflation. It is to protect Old Age Pensions and Family Allowances against inflation that the Government introduced indexation many years ago.
Yet today we are debating a Bill the Government introduced that will take away that same protection he was so magnanimously talking about.
The Government is using this legislation as a means to get senior citizens to practise restraint. 1 suggest, Madam Speaker, that the Government is completely out of touch with reality because pensioners have already been practising restraint in every aspect of their daily lives. They already have to restrain themselves from buying many of the basic items of food and clothing. Yet the Government has the audacity to ask them to practise restraint and to do without that added 4 per cent cost-of-living increase they so desperately need to keep up with the continually rising price of food, clothing, transportation and shelter.
There are 100,000 poor and near-poor affected by this proposed legislation. 1 am particularly concerned about the single pensioner who will be most affected by the Bill. Women are the majority in this category and have only the old age pension to fall back on if their spouses are no longer living and they have not been employed in the labour force at any time in their lives. Single pensioners who receive only the basic old age pension of S246.92 per month will be the ones who will fall further and further behind, while those eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement will have their supplements to assist them in keeping pace with the rate of inflation and, therefore, will have a somewhat small chance of stabilizing their standard of living.
But what about the 50 per cent of pensioners who receive only the basic pension? They are among those who have worked all their lives to ensure, hopefully, a comfortable retirement-seniors who have scrimped and saved over the past 30, 40 and 50 years; seniors who have invested their hard-earned dollars over the years in order to be able to live above the poverty line in retirement; seniors who have sacrificed those many evenings out, a new winter coat or a new car, so that their retirement savings could grow and build for the future.
Our senior citizens of today are the people who built the country to what it is now. They are the people who are the backbone of our great nation. They are the people who defended our borders in two world wars to give us the freedom and democracy we enjoy today. They are the people who survived the bread lines and the soup kitchens of the great depression. They are the people who toiled and sweated through 10, 12 or 14-hour days so that their children could enjoy some of the luxuries of life they never had when they were young. We
cannot ignore the contribution our seniors have made to Canada and to us as individuals, but if the Bill is allowed passage through the House, we will be doing just that.
The Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has said time and time again that she cares about our elderly, that she cares about their needs being met and that they are being properly looked after. If she really cared, if she was really concerned, the Hon. Minister would have prevented Bill C-131 from being introduced in the House, so that seniors could still have a fighting chance to maintain their standard of living as they have tried to do in the past.
The Government is not only limiting the indexation of the old age pension through the Bill; it is also limiting the indexation of personal income tax to 6 per cent under amendments to the Income Tax Act. That means the Government is not only making our seniors pay once, it makes them pay twice; it goes back for more through the Income Tax Act. This is hardly the response one would expect from a caring Government or a caring Minister.
Instead of helping them at a time when they need it most, the Minister has gone along with the wishes of her Cabinet colleagues who have only just begun to realize that it is time to restrain the extravagant and ostentatious spending in which their Government has been engaged for the past 14 years. To save their own political necks, they pick on the most vulnerable section of Canadian society to pay for the gross mismanagement of an economy gone wild. The Government has a cold-hearted, callous attitude toward the senior citizens of the country, not the warm-hearted one it claims to have.
Our seniors deserve far better treatment for their many years of service than the Government is giving them in this legislation. They have fought for the country, they have helped it grow into a great nation, and they have raised a nation of workers who are struggling to maintain the standard of living established by their fathers and mothers. It is time the Government repaid them for so many years of service rather than penalize them for being over the retirement age.
We are all in favour of the Government restraining its spending, but surely the mistakes of the Government should not be a burden the elderly are expected to bear. Let us look at how much the Government will be saving by limiting indexation on pensions-$10 million. This is not a great sum when we put it against an increasing deficit of almost 1,300 times that amount. There are many other areas in which the Government could save this $10 million. Just to give one small example, in the last fiscal year the Government is reported to have spent $10.5 million on what it terms "hospitality", meaning food, entertainment and liquor, hardly essential items for the bureaucracy during times of advocating restraint. The amount it spent on hospitality is just over the amount of money it will save through the Bill on the backs of our senior citizens.
This is at a time when over 600,000 of our elderly are living in abject poverty. Yes, I have spoken to these people. I have seen what they put in their shopping carts in the grocery store.
I have visited with them in their homes. I know their fears of
November 30, 1982

wondering how on earth they will make ends meet. The Government should be looking at itself for ways to save this sum of money. Where is the equity? Where is the fairness of saving money at the expense of the elderly who have contributed so much to the country? Where is the protection of which the Prime Minister spoke last week? What has happened to the Liberal philosophy of looking after those who cannot look after themselves?
At a time when we are faced with the worst recession in 50 years, the Government is taking money out of the pockets of those who need even more, instead of helping them when it is obvious they require all the assistance they can get. I should like to see the Government explain to all senior citizens why they should be the ones to give up so much so that the Government can save so little. This is a savings of a few million dollars pitted against a climbing deficit of over $100 billion. It will not even make a dent in this outrageous, continually growing deficit.
All the Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the spouses' allowance payments put together account for only 2.5 per cent of the nation's gross national product. That is a drop in the bucket for the Government. But the money lost to senior citizens is worth much more to them. To them it means a lowering of their already falling standard of living, more and more hardships for them to face, and more financial burdens to bear for those who no longer have the strength or the determination to cope with these problems.
What about the future? What about the seniors of tomorrow? We are only too painfully aware, or should be aware, of the fact that there will be a decreasing number of workers to pay into pension funds which will have to look after an increasing number of pensioners. There will be a major drain on the old age pension, the Canada Pension Plan and retirement plans in about 30 years when those of the baby boom generation hit the age of 65. There will not be enough people paying taxes or contributing to private and public pension plans to support the drain on revenues expected at that time.
We need to prepare for the future, and we can do it in a number of ways through pension reform and re-educating the young people of today so that they will not have to rely on Government-subsidized old age pensions for their retirement. Fortunately, a switch to alternative retirement income is already beginning to happen. The number of people eligible for GIS is decreasing steadily despite the increase in the over 65 population. In May, 1978 53.9 per cent of pensioners qualified for GIS while in May, 1982 only 49.9 per cent required the same benefits. But we need to do more.
The Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare has spoken many times of bringing in a green paper on pension reform, but we have yet to see it. 1 urge the Minister to consult with all Parties to bring about immediate discussion on pension reform. We can no longer afford further delay in an area where there is such urgency. We must consider areas of reform which will take us away from assuming greater public debt. There must be determination to progress and meet this challenge of the future.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
In conclusion, the younger generation of today has to be given direction now to prepare itself for retirement 25, 30 or 40 years down the road. We must concern ourselves with providing incentives and direction so that those who follow will be able to provide for themselves in the future. I hope the Government will turn away from penalizing the present senior citizens with legislation to limit indexing to 6 per cent and 5 per cent and turn its attention toward preparing the youths of today for the future of tomorrow.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often that one has the pleasure of listening to two maiden speeches in a row in this House and to find them both very well done. I wish to compliment the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt) and the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). I cannot, because of the tradition of the House, quarrel with anything that was said by either one, and I would not want to do so in any case. But next time, it will be fair game.
I do not rise with pleasure to speak on Bill C-131. The remark usually made by speakers at the commencement of a speech is: "It gives me great pleasure to rise to speak on Bill" such and such. This Bill gives me a great deal of pain and anger. Bill C-131 should not be before the House. In fact, it should never have been written. Why the Government decided to introduce this kind of legislation at this time is beyond me.
We are in favour of restraint. Our Party believes in restraint, but we have never intended that restraint to be applied against senior citizens in this country. Yet here we have Bill C-131. One gets the impression that the Government looked around to see where it could make some cuts. The Government could not cut anything from de Havilland, Canadair or PetroCan, nor could the Government get a cheap price on Petrofina. The question was, where could the Government cut? It must have thought about the cheques being sent to the old age pensioners. They cannot hurt them much, so they apply their cuts to them and to the civil servants.
Let me digress for a moment. There seems to be some confusion in the House about this triad of Bills that we have in this broad area of six and five. Bill C-124, which the Conservatives supported last July, was a six and five pay raise cap. This Bill also had a provision for a pay cut Members of Parliament. Bill C-124 was supported by the Conservatives, moved by the Liberals and opposed by the New Democratic Party.
Bill C-131 now comes before us and it is to cap the indexation of old age pensions. It is not an indexation of supplementary pensions, but to cap the indexation of old age pensions.
Bill C-133 is to follow. This Bill is to cap the indexation of pensions paid to federal civil servants who have retired, Members of the Armed Forces, members of the RCMP and others. The hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) mixed these Bills, unintentionally I am sure, when he was speaking on Bill C-124. Votes are taken separately on each of these Bills and it is quite possible to vote yes for one and no for the other, which is what the Conservatives are doing. We voted

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
yes on Bill C-124, which capped pay raises for civil servants and had a pay cut in it for Members of Parliament, and we intend to vote against Bill C-131.
I like to speak on a Bill such as this because the constituency from which I come is the senior citizen capital of Canada, the retirement city of Victoria. I was pleased when in 1980 a former colleague of ours from Leeds-Grenville put a question on the Order Paper asking what constituencies in Canada had the highest percentage of senior citizens, persons 65 years af age and over. The answer tabled in due course was that the ten constituencies with the highest percentage of senior citizens, persons 65 years of age and over, in descending order were: Victoria, B.C.; Vancouver Centre, B.C.; Joliette, Quebec; St. Paul's, Ontario; and Winnipeg North Centre. If I could pause there for a moment, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, (Mr. Knowles) unfortunately is not in the House today. I am sorry he is not here because he would not like this Bill, I can assure the House. He is well known on all sides of the House for his tremendous, indeed indefatigable, efforts on behalf of pensioners. Personally, I owe him quite a bit of gratitude for the number of times I have been able to ask for his advice and clarification on very obtuse points that one comes across in Government Bills at times. I suspect it is his presence that attracts senior citizens to Winnipeg North Centre in such great numbers.
I will continue with the list of the sixth to the tenth constituencies having the highest number of senior citizens living in them. Next comes Mount Royal, Quebec; Hamilton West, Ontario; Vancouver Quadra, B.C.; St. Henri, Quebec; and Don Valley West, Ontario.
As Hon. Members will notice, the Province of British Columbia has three of the ten constituencies having the highest percentage of senior citizens living in them, Victoria being right at the top. That, I suppose, is partly because of the salubrious climate. But the people of Victoria, of which 22,500 are old age pensioners, have grown accustomed to their presence and have found an ability in them to be a productive and an outgoing part of the community.
I might just say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) that the New Horizon grants have been of good value in Victoria. They are well used and they do much to give a quality of life to the senior citizens which they otherwise would not have.
However, our society is now evolving differently. We have fewer people in the younger one-third of the population and even more people in the older, top one-third of the population. We will have to address the problem of life after 60. We will have to address leisure time and what to do with it. Technology is finally getting its point across that automation and the use of robots in factories will enable production to carry on without a great deal of personal effort. We will have to look at shorter work weeks and shorter work days. This in turn leads to more leisure time, yet we seem not to be looking at that. Leisure time is something that must be addressed and I hope that in future Bills we may see something in that order.
It is strange the way this Government has moved since the first old-age pension was introduced in Canada in 1926. It was a pretty meagre pension in those days. It was subject to a means test and a person had to be 70 years of age. The amount paid was $20 a month.
Then things began to improve a little for old age pensioners. I recall that my father had prepared for his own old age in a rather modest way. He found it great amusement, because he was almost a life-long Conservative, to have a Liberal Government suddenly present him with an old-age pension at age 70. In the very month that he reached 70 years of age, the means test was done away with and my father received his pension, about which he chuckled in the years left to him. We recall when the Conservative Government was headed by the former right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, who pointed out that pensions were in no way keeping up with the inflated cost of living. His Government brought in a decent pay increase for old age pensioners.
From there we go on to Liberal times in the 1960s and eventually we come to the indexation of old age pensions, a measure suggested by the Hon. Robert Stanfield in the election campaign of 1972. The Liberals who opposed it, saying that it was impractical, brought it in shortly after the election. There was a steady effort made by the Government to improve the lot of senior citizens. But the government began to change its policy during the last five years. We saw the introduction of one small restriction and subsequently other restrictions which I will elaborate on later.
This particular proposal is a first. The Guaranteed Income Supplement has been established and we now see a Bill which will significantly change the complexion of the senior citizen's old age pension by having it indexed to only 6 per cent unless the pensioner is drawing the Guaranteed Income Supplement. The fact that we have two categories of old age pensioners will be even more pronounced. There are those who draw the basic pension and those who draw the basic pension plus the old age supplement. The current scale of the Old Age Security payment is $246.92 per month for a single person. The Guaranteed Income Supplement, which applies to pensioners whose income is at a certain level, which I believe is below $8,500, is $247.89. The total of these two pensions is $494.81, which amounts to an annual payment of $5,937.72. Of course, that is the current amount and it will increase as quarters go by.
As individuals approach their retirement years, they have understood and become accustomed to the fact that senior citizen pension incomes were indexed to the cost of living. Therefore, they were able to plan for their so-called golden years in the knowledge that they would have a certain amount of money. If individuals could anticipate receiving $494.81, and perhaps another small income, the old age pensioner would be able to pay for an increase in his rent, transportation costs or health care because of the indexing factor in the pension.
November 30, 1982

As well, those who are on the old age pension without the supplement also expected that their pension would be increased according to the consumer price index. It turns out that this will no longer be the case. They will have to lower their standard of living and this is extraordinarily difficult when you are a senior citizen. It usually entails lowering the cost of accommodation.
I have seen the situation quite frequently in Victoria that when a pensioner's income will no longer meet the rent they have to find a place where that pension can meet the rent. This means giving up what might have been a two-bedroom suite and moving into a one-bedroom apartment, or indeed a single room. This is perhaps the most demeaning of all the experiences one runs into as a result of this demeaning Bill.
How did we arrive at this pass under the benevolent and capable current Minister of National Health and Welfare, who has always given me a very clear impression that she favoured the welfare of senior citizens? Yet she has brought in this Bill which will obviously affect the standard of living of senior citizens, particularly those who do not draw the Guaranteed Income Supplement. I believe that an earlier speaker, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), mentioned that it is customary in other parliamentary systems for ministers to resign if they cannot look after their portfolio or department, cannot either introduce suitable policies or maintain the ones in existence. That is not the case with this Government. A Minister writes a Bill, introduces it in the House and whips everyone into line to vote for it.
I cannot avoid mentioning that only one Liberal, apart from the Minister, has stood up to give his opinion. I would particularly like to have the Member, who in essence is my MP when I am in Ottawa, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), stand up and tell us why he thinks it is fair that the retired citizens in his riding should be receiving less disposable income in the future than they are at the present time.
The Minister said in April, when speaking about this possibility: "We have no intention of changing the rules of the game; we want to maintain indexing of the Old Age Security pension and the supplement every three months".
There is another statement which I think shows what the Minister used to say. She seems to be no longer following the same course. On November 4, 1980, at page 4402 of Hansard, the Minister of National Health and Welfare had this to say in answer to a question from the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) when she was in receipt of a document prepared by the Canadian Council on Social Development:
But the universal pension as well as the GIS supplementary pension are indexed fully to the cost of living every three months and these people will be protected fully against these increases.
The Minister has changed. They got to her. Those Members do as they are told in that Party and to heck with the constituency they represent in the broad sense. As a result we are faced with a Bill like C-131 which essentially is the first one that has taken direct aim at the senior citizens of this country and which is resolved to hurt them.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
The Minister has frequently said that pensioners will be getting more money next year than this year. She is quite right to say this if the Government is trying to confuse the general public about whether they will receive more money next year than this year. I agree that they will get more money but it will be limited to an increase of 6 per cent if they are not receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement. If inflation is more than 6 per cent, they will be getting less disposable income.
People in this particular situation will not have the spending power which they have had this year. The Minister has pointed out that this Bill provides for an increase in the supplements that will be large enough to compensate for the shortfall in the pension itself due to the 6 per cent cap. Of course, this means that if we have a 12 per cent increase in the cost of living in 1983, the basic Old Age Security payment will go up 6 per cent and according to my calculations the Guaranteed Income Supplement will have to rise 18 per cent. These are rough estimates since the two pensions are almost equal in value at the present time. The Guaranteed Income Supplement will have to rise approximately 18 per cent if the recipient of the GIS is not to lose any purchasing power. I hope that that will clarify it.
My immediate reaction upon hearing that people on the Guaranteed Income Supplement would get what is called a triple indexation if their estimated 6 per cent was half of the increase in inflation was that the figures were wrong.
The Minister had told us that 55 per cent of the people are drawing the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and I am confused about that because our figures indicate that the number drawing the Guaranteed Income Supplement has been falling. This was thought to be because, as the years go by, more people who have paid into the Canada Pension Plan are coming into that age bracket. Consequently, our figures are quite a bit different.
The private retirement incomes held by recent retirees and the steadily expanding coverage of the Canada and Quebec Pensions Plans are working in there, and it is our impression that considerably under 50 per cent of the people are receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement. However, I expect the Minister will probably have another opportunity to speak in the debate and she may take that opportunity to correct these figures if they are indeed incorrect.
I would like to discuss British pensioners for a while. The Minister will recall that I raised this subject four years ago. They are getting very shabby treatment in Canada. It may be because we are unable to come to some agreement between Canada and Britain. However, it should be pointed out to the general public in Canada that these people are being placed in a terrible position. In 1976 the laws were changed with regard to the length of time one must live in Canada to earn a full pension. It had been ten years but it was cut back.
What I believe to be the first kind of attack on senior citizens by the Government of Canada was that they had to live in Canada for 40 years to get full entitlement. If they

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
came here from another country and lived here for ten years, they would then receive one quarter of the old age pension. The Government said: "We will pay them the Guaranteed Income Supplement which will help them". However, it will not help them beyond the limit of the Guaranteed Income Supplement which, right now, is a maximum of some $247. If one has a full old age pension and no other income, one receives the GIS and is limited to this $247. However, if one came here from Britain ten years ago, one only receives a quarter of a pension, which means that one will then have a total income of $309.62. One will receive an old age pension of $61.73 and the Guaranteed Income Supplement of $247.89; that is, if we are discussing the situation this month. Whereas a Canadian or someone who has lived here for 40 years, a single person, will receive a total of $484.81 from the Government, one who came from Britian ten years ago will only receive $309.62, which is a difference of about $185. These people are definitely not able to live on that amount and it is a very difficult situation in which the Government has put them. This applies only to people who came here after 1976.
I must say that I am rather startled at the number of people who have come to Canada since 1976 and been misinformed by the immigration people as to the rules governing pensions in Canada. These people, in applying for their pensions, find to their horror that they will not receive an old age pension of $246.92 but, rather, one of $61.73, which is pretty awful.
I would like to quote from Hansard of May 27, 1980 wherein the Minister's statement from December of 1978, four years ago, was quoted. It was in reference to an answer to a question I had asked in December of 1978. At that time the Minister stated:
I am investigating the possibility of reciprocity of pension but the Brits really are not helping at all. 1 hope this will be put on the agenda of our two Prime Ministers if they meet very soon-
Parenthetically, they met a week or so later.
-which is what we heard in the press yesterday.
I will continue with the quote of the minister. It reads:
As soon as I know whether it is to be on the agenda or not I will inform the
House and that will, of course, change completely and speed up, I hope, my
course of action. That is my priority. Italy was a priority, Great Britain was
one. Italy is done and I am very proud of it, but I want to unblock the Great
Britain dossier. It is very important.
It was not as important as she thought, I guess, because there is no visible evidence of an inch of progress having been made since that day when she made that statement in the House of Commons in December, four years ago. While it may not mean a great deal to the Government of this country, it means a great deal to the people involved that the governments should get together and accomplish what must be done to prevent these sincere, hard working, elderly people, who have contributed considerably to this country, from suffering.
I expect that this Bill will pass. Despite what we heard a little while ago in the House, if the Liberals produce a Bill and none of them has the courage to vote against it, it passes. There was no way the Government could be defeated last July on the original Bill of this triad, when the pay was capped. There is no way, if it is given the normal course of voting in
this House, that the Bill will fail. I deeply regret the fact that the Bill is here, and I deeply regret my foreboding that it will pass, because it should not pass. It is a cheap, petty attack on those people who should not be attacked in such a fashion.
To be among that group now, one must have been born before November 30, 1917. Those who were born before that date now qualify for an old age pension and those born after do not, but some of them soon will. If one were born before November 30, 1917, that means that one was born during the First World War. One would have had about a good ten years in one's early childhood of living through the twenties, which were referred to as the gay twenties before the word "gay" became totally inappropriate. We will have to think of another description for that decade when Canada was prosperous and going ahead and it seemed to be a great place. We soon found out differently in the 1930s when these people went through a great deal.
The bright promises for the future during the 1920s soon faded in the realities of the 1930s when the Second World War came along. Then there were a couple of good decades when very much progressive legislation came through and the Government seemed to have a realization of the part that was to be played if these senior citizens were to be treated honourably.
However, the Government seems to have become forgetful of the contribution which was made by these people and is now determined to cut its deficit or to be able to afford more purchases for its pet projects. For example, Petro-Canada might want to buy another oil company and it would only take another bit off the incomes of old age pensioners if the Government went forward with it. I think it is a shameful performance and I really look at some of my friends across the aisle and wonder how they can possibly put up with it, but they are.
That concludes my remarks, except to say that I wish we could find another dozen voters somewhere to give the Bill the treatment it deserves, which is defeat.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on this Bill because I remember clearly the June budget and the six and five program that were brought in to attack inflation in Canada. I recall the general acceptance across the country of the six and five program when it was first brought in. In my experience from talking to people in my own constituency, going across the country, going on hot line shows or making speeches across the country, I find there still is considerable acceptance of that program.
I remember clearly that Hon. Members in the Conservative Party took some time to express their support for an attack on inflation. Many of them were directly or indirectly supporting the six and five program. I was grateful for that support, then.
I think that some of the comments that we have heard from the Conservatives and the NDP continue in that vein, but they are healthy reminders to the Government that we must be
November 30, 1982

careful even in an important attack like this one against such a deep economic problem.
I believe the speech that we have just heard from the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) reflects not only his concern for a fight against inflation, but also reflects a genuine compassion for senior citizens and a desire to remind the Government to go gently. I would have welcome that kind of reminder and 1 am sure most of here would.
Because we have been talking this afternoon about principles and about who would be willing to stand up and defend this idea, I want to remind the House that the basic principle still holds true today. We still must engage ourselves in a fight against inflation. It is inflation that causes the worst problem for all Canadians but especially for senior citizens and other people on fixed incomes.
The greatest compassion that we could show to anyone on a fixed income is to provide them with security and stability to meet their cost of living. If people can look ahead to next year and say that the cost of living will hold steady, then that will be the greatest contribution we can make to their lives. It is not misguided to attack inflation. It is not misguided to give pensioners security on the price of food, the price of housing, the price of transportation, the price of clothing and the price of gifts for their grandchildren and their children. Those are things that matter deeply to people, and pensioners want to have the security of stable prices.
In my riding I think pensioners understand that the six and five program is giving them that kind of security and that kind of a target. Senior citizens support the attack against inflation. I have called radio stations and been on hot line shows across the country, including at a station in Victoria, and the question that comes to me constantly from seniors is whether we are going to give them stability of prices and security on the cost of living. People are not asking us about indexing their pension. People are asking whether we are going to get the reason for the indexing under control.
When I talk to pensioners they note that the six and five idea has in the way the Government is applying it, an element of fairness in it. We are applying the six and five idea wherever our reach extends. We are applying it to companies, to prices as well as to wages, and to our social assistance programs. Seniors, in my experience, are saying that it is effective. The six and five program is enlisting co-operation from businesses, from labour, from ordinary people and, most especially, from other Governments. The six and five program is generating an effective attack against inflation.
Finally, seniors have noted that the way we are using the six and five program is helping to rebuild the economy. Pensioners in my area can see how effective, for example, the $3,000 housing grant is becoming in the housing market in Mississauga. That grant is financed by the reallocation of funds from programs like these. We are not simply cutting back; we are using the funds to stimulate the economy in other places, to create jobs and to give people some confidence that there is lasting help. Those are things pensioners want us to do.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
As a Liberal I am very conscious that we must help people who are vulnerable and I am very proud of the record that we have with our various pension programs. I have listened to the recitations and the histories of pension programs in Canada coming from Members on all sides, and I am conscious that it was Liberal Governments that introduced those programs. It was Liberals who gave pensioners a great security net in their pension schemes. But that does not mean that those schemes must constantly be written in stone.
Pensioners today remind us that the basic problem of inflation is that it is attacking their security net. Pensioners themselves tell us that high prices are ruining the security that they have in those pension programs. They are telling us that inflation is the biggest threat they face. They do not regard the six and five program as an attack on senior citizens; they regard it as an attack on the worst problem facing senior citizens and as the logical development in the security of a pension scheme.
Seniors across this country want food costs, rent costs, transportation costs, clothing costs and all the other basic costs brought under control. They have been telling us to not throw money away by constantly increasing the protection they have against inflation, but instead to get inflation down. Senior citizens know that inflation is causing us to lose jobs, causing us to lose the markets for our businesses, causing us to lose the security and comfort that all of us have come to expect from our economy. Senior citizens know that high inflation is creating high interest rates and creating that terrible daisy chain of economic woes that we have been experiencing recently.
Senior citizens are prepared to join in an attack against the root cause of our woes-inflation. They see co-operation from many Canadians and they are prepared to be co-operative in that effort. They have noticed that the federal Government has moved in other sectors, has controlled telephone prices, has controlled CMHC rents, has controlled scores of prices that would otherwise have gone up beyond the 6 per cent ceiling. We have used the money earned from savings in the 6 per cent program to help farmers, fishermen, small businesses and workers in all walks of life.
Above all, senior citizens have seen that the pension program itself is still intact. Next year the pension program will have a 6 per cent increase. The principle of the pensions and their indexing is there. On top of that is the principle that the poorest pensioners are the most protected. That remains intact. By the ingenious joining of the GIS and OAS systems, we have been able to protect those pensioners who need every dollar they can get out of the pension system.
These are basic ideas in this program. I have been asked by people across the way about my principles and whether I will stand up and vote for this Bill. I say I will do it proudly. I do not do that from any sort of external coercion; I do it because 1 am proud of this program.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak to Bill C-131. I find it incredulous and I am amazed that the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), would stand here and say that he will take great pride in voting for this Bill. He is going to vote for this Bill because he supports it. What he really wants to do is cut back on the pay senior citizens are receiving in spite of the fact those senior citizens have done absolutely nothing wrong over the past 10 or 15 years.
The Parliamentary Secretary spoke about compassion. He claims the Liberals are compassionate. When I get into my comments, I will show that the Liberals have not been compassionate with the Canada Pension Plan, inflation or students. Over the last 14 years they have put us in a deficit situation. We have a deteriorating business climate which is getting this country into deep trouble. I will prove beyond any reasonable doubt that they do not qualify for the appellation of being compassionate.
The Parliamentary Secretary spoke about fairness. Howe fair is it to take a senior citizen with just the OAS, S3,000 a year, and limit that to 6 per cent or $180, compared to what is earned by a Member of Parliament, $62,000 and what will amount to an increase of $3,900 next year? That will be our increase, yet we restrict senior citizens to $180. What about the Deputy Ministers who earn $90,000 and next year will automatically receive an additional $5,400 while the senior citizen receives only $180? The Parliamentary Secretary talks
about fairness and compassion. It is a bunch of ballyhoo, and I do not accept it.
He talked about the great Liberal Party that put into place the medicare system, the hospital insurance system and the Canada Pension Plan. That is correct, but the Liberal Party of 15 years ago is not the Liberal Party that stands before us today. It is an entirely different Party.
Classical liberalism, which many of us stand for, the right of the individual to build something and profit from it, has been taken away. With all of their intervention, thousands of statutes and regulations and Crown corporations, they have taken away that right that we all stood for as classical liberals compared to the tyranny of state capitalism.
Members opposite should have a history lesson in economics. I will give it to them. Before 1750 we had in this country state capitalism. At that time there were kings and monarchs. They made all of the decisions with respect to the division of capital and how it was applied to the nation.
In about 1750, as a result of a long process, we got into classical liberalism where the individual owned the capital. The capital was divided into millions of individual segments and the individuals were allowed to make the decisions. When that swept through Europe, it created more wealth than had ever been created in the entire history of mankind. Even the poor in the western nations were far richer than the kings had been under state capitalism.
Since World War II we started with the new form of liberalism, state intervention. After 200 years, from 1750 to 1950, we started on a steady move back to state capitalism, exactly the same point in which individuals found themselves before 1750. We have now ground down to where individual Canadians are at exactly the same point as the peasants were before 1750. That is what the new Liberal Party is doing. Is that something to be proud of? The Parliamentary Secretary should hang his head in shame.
Thirteen Progressive Conservatives have stood up to oppose this Bill because it is wrong. Three Liberals have stood up with a mish-mash of comments on compassion and fairness. It was a bunch of nonsense. There were four NDP who spoke against it. This is another example of the Government since 1968, the new Liberals, the new state intervention. They are the new kings of the land.
The individual Canadian now has to pay the price. There is a special price for our senior citizens who worked hard all their lives. Their standard of living is dropping and will drop more if we do not get these people opposite out. 1 am pleased to report that senior citizens are banding together. They see the threat of the current Liberal Party. They will be active in the next election and will do their part to throw them out.
This Bill is part of the six and five program. Wait until January when the new rules come in. Members will speak for 20 minutes and there will be a 10-minute question period. I can hardly wait until Members opposite read their departmental speeches. The odd one prepares his own speech, but most
November 30, 1982

are prepared for them. We will have a lot of fun. Members will have to know what they are talking about. I can hardly wait.
The Government is virtually extorting from senior citizens their proper fee. Let me talk about Bill C-133. All during their careers, retired public servants paid into the pension plan. They paid an extra 1 per cent pursuant to a signed and negotiated contract. They paid that amount and now they are entitled to indexing at the rate of inflation. They paid an extra 1 per cent-pursuant to a signed contract and they are entitled to the benefit. The Government took the money, put it into a special-well, it did not put it into a special account but there is a bookkeeping entry. The money was frittered away, but it is on the books and there is a surplus of about $14 billion, if I remember correctly. But the Government is not going to honour the contract, and that is extortion. If private enterprise did that, those guys opposite would be up yelling and screaming. But because their Cabinet has done it, they are going to stand up and vote for this Bill, and all their claims to independence do not mean a sweet thing because they are not independent. They are being called to support a Cabinet which should not be supported. If they really represented the true interest of their constituents they would let the people have a choice. We know what the people will do, they will turf them out.
When any of these Bills are being discussed, Mr. Speaker, we should never forget about where we were in this country. Let us go back to 1968. We had a small national debt, just a drop in the bucket. We had a balanced budget, yet even with that we had a health care system second to none. We had hospital insurance and a medicare system under which the doctors were happy. We had post-secondary education for thousands upon thousands of people who were able to come from both the farms and the cities and go to university. We had a first class agricultural industry which exported to ail countries of the world. We had a manufacturing infrastructure in Ontario second to none. Our standard of living was second from amongst of the OECD countries, which meant we were second in the world. That is what we had in 1968 and we could truly be proud. Not only did we have Old Age Security, we had a Canada Pension Plan and a regular retirement benefits program for senior citizens under which they could feel secure and know that they had done well throughout their life, built a nest egg for their retirement, and they could look forward to their old age. There is no doubt we were one of the finest countries in the entire world.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what has happened? Have the citizens changed? Did we do something to deserve being where we are today?
Let me tell you where we are today, Mr. Speaker. The first thing the Government did was to change the rules so that Members of this House were no longer in control of the purse strings. During the normal course when the Estimates come along, they are automatically approved. It does not matter
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
what this House or the standing committees do. From the moment financial accountability to this House ended, you can chart the deficit as it went up in direct proportion to what the Government has been doing to this House since then. As a result we are no longer second in our over-all standard of living, we are thirteenth. We are in fiftieth place in our financial standing in the Euro-money market. So practically everyone else in the world is doing better than us.
Government Members always stand up and say, well, inflation is affecting the entire western world and we are trapped just like everyone else is. Well, that is true, but why have we dropped from second place to thirteenth? It is because of their policies over there, nothing more. Let us not fool ourselves. When they force this Bill through, they are forcing through a law which breaks a signed and sealed contract. The federal civil servants delivered their end of the contract, they paid the extra 1 per cent. In all fairness, Mr. Speaker, the Government should say that, well, we have taken your 1 per cent for all these years and now we are breaking the contract, so we will give you your 1 per cent back. That would be the fair thing to do, but the Government is not doing that. In fact, it is continuing to collect the 1 per cent from the employees today. So federal civil servants are being forced to pay the 1 per cent, but if they have to retire today they are not going to get the extra inflation benefits. Surely the Government should be consistent; if it is going to break the contract, it should give them their money back.

I said that in 1968 we had almost a negligible national debt. It is now over $140 billion, and if we add in the Government's contingent liabilities for the guarantees it has given to the Massey-Fergusons, the Domes and the Petro-Cans of the world, the exposure is well over $200 billion. We have gone from balanced budgets to a deficit of over $24 billion a year or $2 billion a month, Mr. Speaker. The interest to service the debt is going to be about $17 billion or $18 billion. As I have said before, that is not insignificant because it concentrates wealth in the hands of people who are already wealthy.
If someone has $1 million, they are not going to put it out into business; they are going to lend it to their own Government and get 19.5 per cent, as they did last year. That has the effect of making the rich even richer, and it does away with our middle class. When we do away with our middle class, Mr. Speaker, we will lose that enormous buffer against extremism, whether it be political, ideological or religious extremism. As the Government destroys the middle class, it destroys Canada, and we will end up like the Third World countries where there is a small group of the incredibly rich and a huge group of poor.
Is that what Liberalism is about? Is that what compassion is about? Is that the fairness that the Hon. Member for Mississauga North speaks about? He stands up and is proud of that

system. I would like to see what the senior citizens of his riding think of that.
How did the Government do this, Mr. Speaker? Canadians are a bright people, but as they get more education it seems that this Government wants to impose more regulation on them. Is it not ironic that when Canadians were developing and building this country-under Conservative Governments and old Liberal Governments, the classic Liberals-we did not have to have regulations and rules to affect our people. Now that we have them educated-we have probably the highest standard of education in the world-we think they need to have millions of statutes and regulations to hold them down. That is what Liberals have done to the people of this country. They got us into this enormous trouble, for which we are now paying a severe price. They did it by offering very attractive programs in practically every area, including many under the sole jurisdiction of the Provinces. At the same time as it offered these programs, the Government kept taxes low and borrowed the difference. It is great at the start. Maybe 5 per cent of tax revenues go to service interest on the debt. It is 10, 15 or 20 per cent and now it is up to 30 per cent. At 30 per cent the Liberals are alarmed and want to cut back. Suddenly, they want to draw the line at 30 per cent. Why 30? Why not let it go to 35, 40, 50 or 100 per cent? If Liberalism means that programs can be offered, based on low taxes and the difference borrowed, then why is 30 the magic figure?
Perhaps the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) will direct his mind to that question. Why is 30 per cent of the tax revenue going to service the debt? Why is that the point chosen to cut it off, rather than 25 per cent or 15 per cent? What does the Hon. Member think the ideal figure is? I should like his views on that.
Senior citizens are being asked to cut back. Those are the people who will have to use the medicare system and the hospital insurance system more, as they grow older. As early as last year, by cutting out the revenue guarantee, which was really a fiction, the Government cut back on contributions to the Provinces by several hundreds of millions of dollars. As a result, the Provinces cut the flow of money to hospitals and doctors, and now senior citizens will have to pay more out of their own pockets for these services.
It is a two-edged sword, Mr. Speaker, and senior citizens get it both ways. I see the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is shaking her head. All revenue sharing was fiction.

work, provided the Government uses both sides of the equation. In short, Keynes says that when there are tough times the Government should borrow to stimulate the economy. I would like to draw to the attention of Members on the other side that none of us would be supporting Bill C-131 if it were in isolation. But we must remember that it is part of an over-all package to control inflation. Bill C-131 is part of a comprehensive plan. It is part of an over-all package for economic recovery, and it cannot be taken in isolation. If that were true, none of us could support this action.
What we are trying to do with this legislation and through the six and five program is to reduce the burden on the taxpayer. We are asking everyone to make a contribution, except those who are in the greatest need. We are saying that we can reduce the burden on the taxpayer and it is a matter really of non-contributory versus the contributory plan. We are looking at such things as the GIS, the Old Age Security and the Canada Pension Plan. We know which of those are contributory and which are non-contributory. We know that those programs designated to assist people in the greatest need are the GIS and the child tax credit programs. What we must do, above all, is to defeat inflation. Equally important, we must restore economic growth. If we do not restore economic growth, there will be an even greater pressure on the social programs than there is now. Therefore, our six and five program and Bill C-131, which is part of the whole package,
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
are to fight inflation but they are also to restore economic growth.
The reason I feel that I can support this legislation is that the Government is asking for a small contribution from all of those who benefit from programs funded by the taxpayer and from those who work for the taxpayer. What are the choices? A bigger deficit? A burden on the taxpayer? I do not think so. But today, if we think about it, who is in greatest need? I have no doubt that all of the things we have heard about the plight of the elderly today are true. I agree times are difficult for them. Times are difficult for them because they have lost stability, mainly because of the economic times which have arisen, principally because of inflation. Who is in the greatest need?
