speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I wonder whether that Hon. Member has ever heard of evolution. We have to change with the times. The economic times of today in the world are different. We have had to change. If we all contribute today, we will be able to provide for a brighter tomorrow. Certainly, those with the greatest interest in the ability of taxpayers to fund these programs are retired. We seem to forget what this Bill is all about. This Bill is all about helping those people least able to help themselves. There is no question that there is a crisis in our national life. The Government has called upon all Canadians to share in a determined effort to fight inflation and bring it down. It is only right that those Canadians who are not in need are entirely prepared to share in the serious sacrifices that are required to bring our current economic crisis under control. It requires the co-operation of Canadians to overcome this formidable challenge.
At a time when the Government is calling upon Canadians to tighten their belts and strive even harder to overcome the

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
evils of inflation, I find it gratifying to see that the Government's total commitment to protecting and ensuring that those benefits it wishes to give through those programs that are designated to assist our fellow Canadians most in need will not be reduced. One can see that this is provided for in the Bill.
The Government is proposing in the Bill which is before us today to limit indexation of the Old Age Security benefits to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. I want to emphasize the point that full indexation of these benefits will resume on January 1, 1985. However, this Bill also ensures that the lowest income pensioners will be fully protected from the limitation of the indexing factor. This fact seems to have been forgotten. The Guaranteed Income Supplement for pensioners with lower income will continue to be fully indexed. In addition, everyone receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement will receive an extra increase to fully offset the limitation of indexation of basic Old Age Security payments. This same protection from the limitation of the indexing factor will also be extended to recipients of a spouse's allowance.
When this is all put into context with what we have heard from the Opposition so far, one sees that their allegations that the Government is removing benefits and reducing what those in the greatest need have are false. That is not the fact.
I would like to concentrate on these particular aspects of the Bill. Low income pensioners will continue to receive the benefit of fully indexed pensions. This means that pensioners in receipt of a Guaranteed Income Supplement or a spouse's allowance will receive a benefit that will continue to be indexed to the Consumer Price Index. In addition, the benefits will be increased by an amount corresponding to the loss associated with the reduced indexation on the basic income.
This approach maintains the income guarantees of the present program. In fact, there are now some pensioners who are just above the qualifying income level for the Guaranteed Income Supplement who will be eligible for this benefit because of the limited indexation of the basic pension. I want to emphasize that no pensioners loses out. This is an important fact which the Minister has been trying to point out. This is the purpose of the program.
As I have said, those who are not in need are being asked to make some contribution in the fight to reduce inflation. This is the purpose of the six and five program. Those benefits which pensioners have received in the past will be retained during 1983 and 1984. They will continue to receive them in 1985 when full indexation is restored to the program as a whole. We can be proud that the guarantees made to low income pensioners are being honoured and fully protected by this Government.
It is most encouraging that in spite of the economic constraints, after objectively analyzing our social policies for older Canadians, the Government has been able to maintain a firm stand and give assistance where it is most needed. This legislation is most important because it emphasizes the Government's continuing concern and commitment to the needs of our persioners. All Canadians have seen the effects of recession and spiralling inflation on the economy. However, some groups, such as low income pensioners, are particularly
vulnerable to the impact of inflation. Even at a time when great restraint is in order, it is reassuring to see that the Government is very aware of the plight of those older Canadians who are most affected by inflation.
In Canada, at the end of the nineteenth and into the twentieth century, the increasing level of industrialization led to a change of lifestyle and weakened the traditional extended family responsibilities. The individual increasingly became responsible for saving and providing for his or her own retirement. At the same time, the new industrial structure meant that increasing numbers of older workers were being forced into retirement. Poverty among the elderly was widespread because few pension plans existed and personal savings for retirement were inadequate. Increasing pressure was brought to bear on the federal Government to aid the elderly who lived in poverty.
The federal Government assumed the major responsibility for the welfare of the elderly in 1951. Section 94 of the British North America Act was amended in that year to authorize Parliament to make laws in relation to old age pensions.
It was only 16 years ago in December, 1966, that the Guaranteed Income Supplement Program for Old Age Security recipients was approved. In January 1967, pensioners born on or before December 31, 1910, who had no other source of income, became eligible for a 40 per cent supplement to the Old Age Security pension. The Guaranteed Income Supplement Program was initially designed to provide financial assistance to those persons who would not be eligible or would not fully benefit from the introduction of the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans in 1966.
I have lived long enough to remember the days when we lived in the so-called gold watch syndrome when all that one received after working many years was perhaps a handshake and a gold watch. These earning-related social insurance programs providing for the income protection in the event of death, disablement or retirement of labour force members, offered no benefit to those already retired and only limited benefits to those retiring during the ten-year phase-in period. We had problems even at that time.
The Guaranteed Income Security was to be a transitional program gradually phasing out as the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans were phased in. The extent of the Guaranteed Income Security Program when it was first introduced was to provide a basic minimum income to those pensioners who had no other source of income. It served as a floor below which pensioners' income could not fall. The Guaranteed Income Security was never intended to provide an adequate income but was simply designed to financially assist pensioners with little or no income who could not fully benefit from the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans.
It was soon realized, howver, that these earning-related plans would not replace the need for income assistance to the elderly. Therefore, the Guaranteed Income Security was made a permanent feature of the Old Age Security Program. This became effective in 1971.
November 30, 1982

Since 1971, the guaranteed income approach to alleviating poverty in this country has been acknowledged as one of the most important advances in social policy in Canada's history. It is a way of ensuring that the basic needs of pensioners with no income or very limited income other than the basic Old Age Security pension can be met without subjecting them to the indignity of a means test.
Another significant change in the program occurred when, in 1975, a second income-tested benefit, the spouse's allowance, was introduced. This income-tested benefit was payable to the 60 to 64 year old spouses living with Old Age Security pensioners. The program was intended to meet the needs of many married couples in Canada who were being forced to live on a single Old Age Security pension and a Guaranteed Income Supplement, because only one spouse was over 65 and eligible for these benefits. In the traditional pattern of marriage in this country, the husband was generally older than the wife, and very often, especially in the case of older couples, the husband had been the only wage-earner. It was quite reasonable, therefore, to ensure that the minimum income needs of the couple would be basically met through this program. It did not make much sense, for example, that a couple receiving Old Age Security program benefits might also have to seek provincial social assistance to meet basic income needs.
The Old Age Security program and, in particular, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, are widely perceived to be the only practical means of ensuring that Canada's elderly have adequate incomes. This program now plays a vital and important role in Canada's retirement system. Indeed, the Guaranteed Income Supplement is the only part of the retirement income system that presently guarantees a minimum level of income to virtually all of Canada's elderly population.
The cost of improving benefits in any program is not negligible, but the importance of these income-tested programs has been fully recognized and protected. In 1979, and again in 1980, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and Spouse's allowance programs were enriched. The benefit rates were increased by $20 per pensioner household on January 1, 1979 and again by $35 in July of 1980. The role of these programs is so important to those pensioners requiring this additional financial assistance, that in those years when inflation was inflicting severe financial difficulties, the Government took decisive action to increase its commitment to these people.
The Government is striving to protect the improvements that have been made thus far in our effort to fight poverty and to ensure that our elderly population is guaranteed a basic minimum income level. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has repeatedly said, sacrifices by those who can throw a lifeline to those struggling with inflation and economic hardship must be made. Our country will recover from the ravages of inflation. That is what the program of six and five is all about and that is what this Bill is trying to do. It is trying to ensure that we will succeed with this program. I think one of the major reasons we are hearing so much criticism from the Opposition is the fact that the program is succeeding, and the fact that
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
inflation is being reduced and these elderly people will eventually be better off.

I believe that we can all take great pride in maintaining and fully protecting the rights of our low-income pensioners in these hard times. We have said over and over again that this is the Government which has been known for doing just that. The social contract between the Government and the people of Canada has not been broken, nor will it be broken. We in Canada can be proud of the system of retirement income planning that presently exists, a three-tiered retirement income system to which this government is fully committed. The first tier of the retirement income planning system is the Old Age Security program. It is the cornerstone upon which a solid foundation for the future retirement of every Canadian can be laid. It provides a guarantee that pensioners will receive a minimum level of income when they retire.
The second tier consists of benefits from the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. These Plans are part of the compulsory contributory social insurance plans which I mentioned earlier, plans which enable members of the labour force to acquire and retain protection for themselves and their families against the loss of income due to retirement, disability or death.
Finally, the third tier of our retirement income system consists of private income sources such as employer-sponsored pension plans, registered retirement savings plans, and the other savings and acquired assets of a lifetime.
It is probably important that we recognize that these later acquired assets of a lifetime are one of the major things which are being hurt by inflation. People who have saved diligently, who have put money away for a rainy day because of inflation, are finding that these dollars are no longer sufficient.
We have said earlier, as did my colleague the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher), that the Government is doing its best to control those prices over which we have some jurisdiction, but it is incumbent on all of those who are earning and all of those who are not in need to try to make some contribution to this fight against inflation. Therefore, we see these three components, old age security, public pension plans and private resources, diminishing as inflation continues. Therefore, the fight against inflation, the reduction of inflation, enhances our savings on which we have been

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
counting to support us as we grow old, when we are no longer capable of earning.
These three components constitute the framework of the three tier retirement income planning system in Canada. Retirement income is planned over a lifetime and this Government, by confirming its commitment to the Old Age Security program has shown great strength and leadership. This Government has reaffirmed that the concepts of universality and indexation shall and must be protected and retained for our present and future generations.
I do not think I can put this in any stronger context than by saying that the Government is concerned about others. We are concerned about those people who have been so eloquently described by the Opposition as people in need. It is satisfying to me that the need has been identified on both sides of the House. This Government has recognized that need through all these years and has established programs to look after these needs.
Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we will continue to make sure that those in greatest need in this country will be looked after. They will not be forsaken. I hope they will be reassured by the statement from Members of the Government who are supporting this legislation and that they will not be frightened into thinking something is being taken away from them or that they are going to lose what they were counting on having.
This legislation, not only this Bill C-131 but the total package of legislation of six and five, is to protect our senior citizens and to make sure that what they get from the Government and what they have saved through their lifetime will meet their needs.
I would like to reaffirm that this concept of universality and indexation shall and must be protected and retained for our present and future generations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might just begin my comments again by saying that I have been waiting a long time to speak on this Bill as the debate on it has progressed over the several afternoons and evenings. It would be a much happier occasion if we were addressing a Bill which was improving the lot of pensioners, and establishing a benefit, instead of making it more difficult for our senior citizens to make their way in these difficult economic times. Pension reform will have to wait until after the November 1981 Budget, and after the borrowing Bills, the sports pool and several other bits of legislation which will come forward between now and the end of the session are taken care of.
Bill C-131 proposes to limit the costs of living increases in old age pensions to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984 without regard to the rate of inflation. Exempted from that six and five formula will be those pensioners receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement. By limiting Old Age Security increases to six and five the Government estimates that it will effect savings of some $105 million. I would ask my colleagues and those in the opposite side of this House to keep that figure in mind as we proceed through these comments.
This figure raises a number of issues, not the least of which is the amount of Government spending. The purpose of this Bill and the purpose of the six and five program, of which this Bill is a part, is to save the Government money and to increase its revenues. We on this side say that it is about time that the Government cut back on spending, which has been out of control for quite some time. In our wildest dreams we had not contemplated that the six and five restraint program would begin on pensioners, the persons who have worked throughout their life and now can least afford to bear the brunt of this kind of attack. They are in the front lines while the Government Department heads are free to continue to bring foolish expenditures and frills to the front of spending, but not to the front of the six and five formula which they have so effectively promoted over the last several weeks.
How is it just and equitable, Mr. Speaker, to cut back on pensions while spending millions of dollars on Government
November 30, 1982

advertising? Would it not make more sense to eliminate that advertising and keep the pensions fully indexed? All Members have been receiving a considerable amount of mail to that effect, and 1 am sure my colleagues have been impressed by the spirit that has been shown by senior citizens who say that they will carry their load and pay their way.
Several senior citizens in St. Catharines have written to me saying that they feel it is their duty to participate, to help Canada get out of this difficulty in which the Government has placed us. They are prepared to cut back on the amenities of living; they are prepared to trim their grocery budgets; they are prepared to "make do" another year with their present wardrobes, and they are prepared to encourage others to follow their example.
That kind of spirit, determination and willingness to sacrifice is alive and well in Canada. The Government would be well advised not to squander the last semblance of trust that is in existence now between the people of Canada and this Government.
I do not have to point out that quite apart from the political consequences that would ensue there is a far more serious consequence of loss of faith and trust in this Government itself. Once that trust has been lost, years and years of rebuilding will be required to regain the credibility that is essential in our democratic process.
The spirit being shown by our senior citizens and the trust that they are placing in the federal Government with regard to the six and five program is based on the premise that all Canadians and all levels of Government are going to play their part. Their determination to help Canada is not based on the assumption that they put up with less so that others can spend more.
Unfortunately, that is the case that exists at the present time. Senior citizens receiving the OAS are being asked to forgo $105 million; public service pensioners are being asked to forgo $100 million; Members of Parliament, Senators, House of Commons employees, public servants, RCMP, Armed Forces personnel and employees of Crown corporations are to forgo $800 million. Mothers are being asked to forgo $155 million in reduced family allowance benefits. In addition to these savings, the Government is increasing personal income taxes by $1.3 billion, or an average of $137 per taxpayer. It is slashing, and I emphasize slashing, $582 million from selected Government programs. The restraint total is $3,042 million.
Who really is doing the belt-tightening in this country? We can see that selected sections of our society are forgoing $1.16 billion in reduced salaries, pensions or benefits and that the tax-paying public in general is contributing $1.3 billion more in taxes, for a combined total of $2.46 billion, or better than 80 per cent of the Government's entire restraint program.
The Government, which claims to be leading the way, can only find of this grand sum $582 million to cut from its expenditures. What a shabby example this Government is giving to the people of Canada as it tries to convince them we should try to join together in a program of restraint, a program
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
that is so essential in these difficult economic times, forced upon Canadians by this extravagant Government.
If pensioners are going to be asked to tighten their belts and rally around the flag, then the frills will have to go first, the extravagant use of Jetstars, the Petro-Canada energy advertisements on television and radio and in the newspapers, the free briefcases provided for public servants. The list goes on and on. Also, as we see in today's paper, there are the excess expenditures over last year for Ministers' travelling expenses. These items added up to over $500 million in 1979, so they are not an insignificant amount in 1982.
More important, however, wasteful spending sends a message to Canadians that they are being taken for a ride. Let us look at that for a moment. When the press continues to show waste and useless expenditures of this Government, how can Canadians be expected to co-operate? They are being taken for a ride. While they scrimp and save, the Government tends to spend and squander. In these difficult economic times, indeed at any time, the Government cannot afford to leave such an impression with the public, especially the Canadian public, yet we see no action being taken to correct those abuses.
Our Leader has proposed that a parliamentary committee be established to track down waste in Government spending and be empowered to put a halt to it, putting in place a committee or agency to cut such spending where it is found. However, the Government vetoed that proposal. It was not acceptable because it might cut into some of the Government advantages or perks.
We in the Opposition do everything possible to bring forward examples of waste so that the necessary action can be taken, but rarely is anything ever done. Does the Government not care about using the hard-earned money of taxpayers in such a frivolous way?
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway) recently raised a small matter of $6,000 spent on a courier service to deliver maps and photographs to 576 newspapers across this country. Couriers were used instead of Canada Post, incurring this expense of $6,000 for no just reason. In the eyes of some, it might be a small amount. They may say, "What's $6,000?" I emphasize that because I want to tell Hon. Members opposite what $6,000 means. Six thousand dollars represents the amount paid in taxes to the federal Government by two average taxpayers from the City of St. Catharines. In other words, those two taxpayers worked all year, paid their bills, kept up their rent or struggled with their mortgages and contributed $3,000 each to the coffers of this Government. They might have put that $3,000 to much better use themselves, but they thought the Government would use their money, wisely spend it on necessities and as needed. In one single thoughtless moment, that trust was dissipated. The Government squandered what those two taxpayers had contributed after working for a year.
Who could argue that those two individuals could not have put that money to much better use in these days of high

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
interest rates, high mortgage costs, they could have made a contribution to their own welfare instead of having it frittered away in that thoughtless moment.
Who on the Government benches cares if some poor individual in St. Catharines has his or her $3,000 wasted on courier services? To them $3,000 is just a drop in the bucket.
It is the attitude that counts, not the amount. If you do not care about the individual taxpayer's money and if you do not care about the pensioner's forgone cost of living increase, it is high time you packed up and left the job to someone who cares, someone who is prepared to respect the taxpayers' hard-earned money. That is why attitude is of so much importance. As long as this indifference of the Government continues and as long as waste and extravagance are the order of the day, there is no way that we on this side of the House can support a Bill such as the one before us.
Waste and frills must be cut first; trimming and tightening of departmental budgets must be next, then wage, pension and benefit restrictions will follow. Those are the priorities that might logically have been set by the Government, but with this Government, it is the reverse. All we are doing now is cutting the incomes of people to cover the cost of the waste and frills, which means that we are making no headway whatever.
In the interest of relevancy, I am leaving aside the major policy adjustments that could go a long way and should be made if we are to recover from this recession which besets us, but it should be understood that more than restraint alone is needed.
My comments today are clearly not going to change the Government's attitude. The Government will not withdraw the Bill and adopt the proper priority program as it is politically wed to the six and five program. It will see it through no matter what. This being so, and being determined as they are, I want to make a few comments on the Bill in the expectation that when the Bill gets to the committee, level heads will prevail and suggestions will be brought forward into amendments.
We have heard a lot of talk from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on how this Bill does not hurt the needy or affect those in need. That is pure nonsense. The six and five comes into effect for a single pensioner when that pensioner reaches or surpasses an income level of $8,900. Statistics Canada would classify such an individual as being below the poverty line in any major city in Canada, and Canada, and 40 per cent of all Canadians over 65 do live in metropolitan areas with populations of over 500,000.
* (2050)
Married couples join the six and five program when their household income exceeds $15,099, hardly a king's ransom today. In all, some 100,000 pensioners are hovering at these minimum income levels, and they are going to have their cost of living increases frozen at six and five while their rent or mortgage, food, heating and clothing costs will continue to rise, often at a rate in excess of that of inflation. It is evident that using the GIS as a basis for deciding who is in and who is
out of six and five is not satisfactory. The GIS is designed to keep pensioners at a statistically arrived at minimum level needed to live; it is not designed to provide a few extra dollars for movies, dinners out or holiday trips. Accordingly, if the GIS is the lowest acceptable income level, how is the pensioner earning just $1 more than the cut-off level for the GIS better equipped to see his or her pension cut?
I would propose, Mr. Speaker, as an absolute minimum, that the GIS base be scrapped and the Senate committee poverty line be adopted. This is still not being extravagant or generous, but it is a major step closer to putting some truth in the Minister's statement that adoption of the six and five will not affect those in need.
I further propose that money saved by limiting pension increases be specifically allocated to a program clearly identifiable as one of assistance to senior citizens. Whether this be for housing assistance, the New Horizons Program, national park fees or whatever, it can be decided on the basis of need and priority, but it is to assist those who need it. 1 believe it to be absolutely essential that pensioners affected by six and five know exactly the sacrifice they are being asked to make and where the money is to go. This Bill asks everyone to participate except the Government. Let the Government give leadership and then, if necessary, after it has gone through an accepted list of priorities, call on the pensioners and they will respond.
I cannot and will not vote for this Bill, and I will not support any similar effort to shift the burden of economic mismanagement-including resource mismanagement-onto those who have lived their work-a-day lives and are now least able to bear that load.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the Liberal Government has destroyed the compassion that the people of Canada expected from it. The people of this country looked forward to the Minister bringing in the innovations they were expecting. I want to say that I had some personal dealings with the Minister. I went over and discussed programs and policies, and the problems I had with some of my constituents. She told me at that time, "you see, we can be compassionate". I thought at that time, yes, we do have responsible Members of Parliament, responsible Cabinet Ministers who do listen. But now we have a situation where the six and five world has started to take over.
November 30, 1982

No one has mentioned the "Blue Chip Committee". What happened to that six and five program committee headed by Ian Sinclair, President of Canadian Pacific? They were travelling across Canada, expounding the six and five program.
I wonder if Ian Sinclair is still so proud of this program, now that it is starting to affect pensioners across Canada. His salary is in the neighbourhood of $500,000 a year and he is expounding on the six and five program. 1 heard the Parliamentary Secretary talk about how we must have restraint. He knows that just the other day in this House the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced a new Royal Commission into Canada's economic future. The salaries of the people on that Commission are going to be in the neighbourhood of $700 a day. Mr. Macdonald is going to be the Chairman of that Commission, and he created the problem at the time he was Minister of Finance.
This Bill is going to rob over a million pensioners of a portion of their pension which they have earned. Pensioners will lose in two ways. First, they are going to be out of pocket because indexing over the next two years will not keep up with inflation. Inflation this year will be at least 10 per cent, but the indexing will be limited to 6 per cent. The optimists tell us that next year inflation will be 9 per cent or more, but the pensioners' indexing will be limited to 5 per cent.
The Minister claims, Mr. Speaker, that the people hit by this legislation can afford to sacrifice. The Minister knows that in many cases that is not true. The single pensioner's eligibility for the income supplement ends when outside income, including Old Age Security payments, reaches a total of $6,123. That means that a single pensioner with a total income, including the Old Age Security, of $9,200, is still going to lose nearly $300 over two years. The Minister must be aware that an income of $9,200 is already $500 below the poverty line for people living in large cities.
The National Council on Welfare has estimated that over 100,000 poor and nearly-poor Canadians will have their incomes reduced as a result of this legislation.
Another thing the Bill does is to whittle away at the universality of pensions. The Minister has denied this, but it is the truth. The relative value of the Old Age Security, which is universal, is being whittled away while the income tested Guaranteed Income Supplement, is being increased.

As you can understand, Mr. Speaker, our senior citizens are proud. This young couple told me that he needed help. I went down with them to see him. We discussed his problem and I got all the information I could. I tried to find some way of helping. About a week later, through the social assistance programs in the area, I found that some moneys

At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put forward the position of the New Democratic Party on pensions. We believe that an adequate pension is a right and not a privilege, and should be available to all senior citizens regardless of sex, marital status, income class or previous work history. An adequate pension system must have retirement incomes high enough so that retirees remain, as nearly as possible, on the same level as the average standard of living.
These are the kinds of things about which we are talking. Retirement incomes must be above the poverty line regardless of pre-retirement earnings. Pensions must be viewed as intergenerational transfers which connect the standard of living of
pensioners to the general standard of living. Only the federal and provincial Governments are in a position to level taxes, remit the transfers and ensure supporting legislation to guarantee an adequate standard of living. Public pension schemes must be expanded immediately to guarantee a poverty-free, secure standard of living for Canada's two million senior citizens. This is the kind of reform we should be discussing in the House today, not the regressive legislation which the Government brought forward.
It is sad that all the blame should rest on the shoulders of the Minister of National Health and Welfare because she is a very compassionate Minister. Also it is sad that her colleagues have turned on her and left her to defend a policy which we all know is wrong, wrong, wrong. It must be stopped. I urge the Minister in the strongest possible way to rise in the House and request that this piece of legislation be withdrawn immediately, to stop any further suggestion of erosion of the cost of living which many senior citizens know they will be facing in the next couple of years.
There is no guarantee. The Government has given absolutely no guarantee that inflation will come down, yet it is telling senior citizens that they will have to bear the burden of reducing it. The Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) rose in the House and expressed his concern with regard to inflation and how it must be battled to the ground. That same Parliamentary Secretary did not bat an eye when the Government spent over $50,000 promoting its six and five program. It sent out stickers and pamphlets to our constituency offices promoting that program. Little did any of us realize that the old age pensioners of Canada would feel the bluntness and cruelty of the Government.
My Party will be opposing this legislation in the strongest possible terms. The Whip of the Conservative Party asked me whether our speakers would be rising in the House to speak on the Bill. We will rise to speak on it as long as it remains in the House. I have a fear that it may not be for very much longer because the Liberal Government is nervous about what is happening. It is splitting up the Bill, bringing it in one day and hiding it behind a piece of legislation the next day; bringing it forward another day and hiding it once again behind another piece of legislation. Liberal backbenchers do not have the courage or the decency to rise on behalf of their pensioners in their ridings and say that they have had enough and that it is time to get on with some real changes to the pension scheme which will help pensioners rather than take away benefits from them.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to join in the debate this evening. I am certain that we have special responsibilities to speak on behalf of Canadian food producers, on behalf of small business and on behalf of the unemployed, particularly when there are nearly 1.5 million unemployed people at present. Throughout the debate on Bill
November 30, 1982

C-131 we have had an opportunity to speak on behalf of another sector of the community, the people who have contributed so much to the development of economic activity and stability in Canada, namely, our senior citizens.
I have a special interest in senior citizens because I come from an area in southwestern Ontario in which the City of St. Thomas is located, the capital city of my constituency. It may come as a surprise to some Hon. Members that this city of roughly 30,000 people has the second highest number of senior citizens on a percentage basis in the country, second only to the City of Victoria. Although it may not be very relevant to the Bill, I am pleased to have an opportunity to tell the House about that situation. Of course I would not let such an opportunity go by, within reason, without speaking on behalf of the senior citizens in my riding of Elgin.
Although Bill C-131 is only five pages in length, it is over 17 years in backwards thinking. It drives a nail in the heart of the pension program set forth in 1965 by the then Prime Minister, the late Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson. Basically, the Bill is part of the Government's six and five restraint program. It limits increases in the basic old age pension to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. Previously the pension was fully indexed to the rate of inflation as measured by the consumer price index. I firmly believe that was a commitment by the federal Government to the senior citizens of Canada and that it should be kept today.
Currently the old age pension amounts to $246.92 per month. That is hardly a princely sum. Since the pension is adjusted quarterly, by October 1984 pernsioners will be receiving some $274.83 per month if the Bill is enacted. Habitually, senior citizens have always had to bear the brunt of inflation because any adjustment in payment always came three months after the fact. Now they are being told to make a further sacrifice in a nation where inflation has been running at levels beyond 10 per cent. They are being told by the Government that they must accept the six and five restraint program. The gap between the six and five per cent and the real rate of inflation will mean a major sacrifice in the purchasing power of those who receive only the old age pension, those who do not receive any GIS or spouses' allowance. Currently, single persons over the age of 65 do not receive any Guaranteed Income Supplement of spouses' allowance if their total income including basic old age pension is greater the $8,912.40, a level of income $10 below the poverty line for single persons living in metropolitan areas with populations of 500,000 or more.
Today approximately 40 per cent of the 65 and over population live in metropolitan areas which include the Cities of Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary, Winnipeg and Hamilton. Approximately 1.2 million of our senior citizens will be affected. Senior citizens will lose $290 over the next two years if inflation remains at 10 per cent. The other group detrimentally affected by this Bill are the elderly married couples with incomes of just over $15,000. They will suffer a loss of income over the next two years of some $580.

These are the cold facts of the Bill. It will be our senior citizens who will have to bear the full impact of these cuts in their pensions. They will have less money to spend on food and on accommodation, and consequently will have less money on which to live.
It is interesting and yet ironical that at the Liberal policy convention held recently on November 5, 1982, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
When conditions change, Liberals adapt. When old solutions fail, Liberals think anew. Above all else, when economic diversity strikes. Liberals act.

For example, on October 21, Treasury Board announced that certain CBC editorial employees would receive an increase in salary of some 11.5 per cent. Oil prices will increase some 46 per cent over the next two years and natural gas prices will increase by nearly 50 per cent over that same period. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the fact that my hon. friend across the floor is somewhat on edge. I have some knowledge of the input and representations that are being made to me as a Member of Parliament representing the constituency of Elgin. My hon. friend's constituency is within 100 miles of my riding. I am sure that his uneasiness is caused by the fact that he is receiving similar representation from his senior citizen constituents.
I have more latitude because I do not occupy the position of Parliamentary Secretary at the moment. I appreciate that he has a definite obligation to cite the official Government position. I am not hampered by those same guidelines which govern my hon. friend.
The population in Canada of those over 65 has risen by more than 600,000 in the last ten years. This age group has been growing at the rate of 3 per cent per year. This means that without any increase in real benefits the economy will have to grow 3 per cent each year just to provide the necessary revenue to support pensions for these people.
If we do not move on pension reform, we will find ourselves encouraging a far larger public debt. Therefore, we should encourage people to begin planning for their retirement from the moment they enter the labour force. We should encourage people to prepare private pension plans instead of totally relying on the Canada Pension Plan. This would involve making private pensions plans and personal savings instruments such as Registered Retirement Savings Plans more accessible to people who have to move from one job to another, who work part time or drop out of the labour force, as is the case in particular for women in our society who do so to raise families. It means making it possible for women to work in the home to build up pension entitlements in their own right. It means early investing in private pension plans. These are but a few measures which the Government should be undertaking.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said, every year we let slip by without action makes it more and more difficult to avoid real crisis when the elderly become the largest single aid group in the population. If we fail to prepare for it, we will have no excuse because the warning has already been given in the age group statistics of the 1981 census.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
Unfortunately, this Government apparently does not want to prepare for the future. Its complete lack of vision can be seen in this Bill. This Government believes that our senior citizens can do with less. My colleagues and I do not believe that single pensioners earning just over $8,900 or married pensioners earning just over $15,000 can do with any less than they are receiving now.
Again, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) stated in his eloquent speech on November 18, as reported on page 20812 of Hansard:
Senior citizens have already paid the price and we should not ask them to pay more. They should have the right to live well now.
That sums up our position. Our senior citizens have already sacrificed enough for the benefit of our country through their hard work, their dedication, their spirit and, last but not least, through their taxes. In return for their sacrifices this Government now plans to cut many of their pensions as a result of the measures contained in Bill C-131. We look at the way Government issues exemptions and exceptions from its six and five program for other federally controlled sectors of the economy and the way it deals with its close friends. This contrasting treatment is nothing more than blatant hypocrisy on the part of this Government. Our senior citizens deserve better treatment and they need better treatment. Bill C-131 is untimely. It is the cancellation of a contract and the breaking of a promise. It shows complete disregard for a longstanding commitment and is nothing less than an insult to the senior citizens of this country.
The end result of this Bill will be the removal of benefits to a sector of our society which needs it the most at a time when they can afford it the least.
It is a pleasure for me to have an opportunity to speak on behalf of the senior citizens of this country and the senior citizens of my riding of Elgin. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the Government Members opposite as well as the Minister of National Health and Welfare for whom I have a great deal of respect, that, in all honesty, I must indicate that I will certainly welcome the opportunity to vote against this Bill.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the Members opposite this evening, not only the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) but the Member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) and the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) as well.
During the next 20 minutes I would like to clarify some of the statements we have heard about the Bill with which we are now concerned. It seems to me that Members of the Opposition have done a disservice to the elderly in Canada. There have been many misrepresentations about the intent of Bill C-131 toward our elderly. I realize that Members on all sides tend to make speeches in the House which are then mailed to their constituents. I venture to say that if many of the speeches made by Members earlier this evening are mailed to their constituents, they will certainly receive a lot of misinformation.

November 30, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I will begin by commenting on some of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke which he made earlier this evening. He talked about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) not being very compassionate toward the poor of this country or toward the elderly in our nation. In my view, he went on to mix two very important themes which the Liberal Government has had since the speech from the Throne on April 14, 1980. One must take into context what is said when one begins not to differentiate pension reform as it was called in the Throne Speech from Bill C-131 which is before us this evening. He said that, as an example, the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), who is responsible for the Status of Women, should be ashamed that half the women in or near poverty will be adversely affected by the Bill. He said that the Minister of National Health and Welfare had reneged on her commitment to universality of social programs in this country.
Let me just single out those two as examples. The 50 per cent in or near poverty will not be affected by the contents of Bill C-131. We on this side of the House have consistently said that one must understand the social security system that is in place in Canada today to understand properly the context of the six and five program as it relates to our elderly, in particular. It goes without saying that the Old Age Security is the first basis of protection for our senior citizens.
I return to this fact becuse he said that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not a compassionate person, and that was a reflection on the Liberal Party. However, it has been a very compassionate Liberal Party which has largely laid the foundation for our social security system in Canada today. Whether one is in the lower income scale or whether one is an elderly person in this country, the Liberal Party has had a tradition of protecting such people who need help most.
As I said, the first basis of our senior citizens' protection is known as Old Age Security. Any person over the age of 65 is eligible for Old Age Security without any attempt at a means test. In addition, if one is among the 53 per cent who qualifies by a means test, then one is eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement plan. Over the years, of course, we have added a protection relating to the spouses' allowance program for those people who are between the ages of 60 and 65 and who, because of the need for extra money, are eligible for a special allowance.
In discussing those three areas of concern I should say that I think the elderly in Canada should be made aware of exactly what Bill C-131 means to the average elderly person in this country. What we have said is that for the unfortunate 53 per cent of Canadians in need there will be no reduction or capping of the indexation of the Guaranteed Income Supplement plan. That will continue to go with the rate of inflation. The only ones who will be affected by the Bill are those who qualify for Old Age Security on the basis of age.
Let me further explain the need of people who are over the age of 65 who do not qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement. They, too, have a vested interest in the six and
five program which the Government has chosen as an economic course to follow. Lor instance, many people over the age of 65 who qualify for Old Age Security may also qualify for a private pension plan from a private source. The greatest difficulty involving private pension plans has been the annual rate of inflation in Canada. Many Canadians are fortunate enough to have a private pension plan, but when inflation rises by 10 per cent, there are very few who happen to have a cost of living allowance added to their private pension.
Let me separate these three very important factors under Bill C-131. First, it will only affect those people over the age of 65 who qualify only for old age security. Second, it will not affect those who are eligible for spouses' allowance or Guaranteed Income Supplement. They will be maintained, fully indexed, ensuring protection against income loss.
I would like to return to some of the things mentioned by the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke tonight. He spoke of the lack of commitment by the Liberal Party and by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to pension reform, yet if anyone has been active in this whole area, it has been the Minister of National Health and Welfare, along with the Liberal Party. We began with a national conference on pension reform back in April of 1981. We have proceeded by going across this country to explain the idea behind pension reform. We are presently in the process of developing a Green Paper to look after that matter.
1 noticed that the Hon. Member for Elgin also mixed up the two areas, private pension reform and Bill C-131, which is before the House tonight. The Government indicated its commitment to private pension reform in the Speech from the Throne in April of 1980. We have never wavered from our desire for pension reform. I am sure there will be some progress in the reform of private pension systems before the present mandate is finished.
If I can, I want to further explain the rationale linking economic and social policy. It is very important to realize the kind of world in which we were living in the first six months of 1982. I know that many of the Hon. Members of the Opposition tend and wish to blame most of the economic conditions presently facing the Canadian people on the Canadian Government. Let us consider some of the economic conditions existing today and those that existed six months ago in the OECD countries. Six months ago the inflation rate in Canada was running between 10 per cent and 12 per cent. In the U.K. it has been running at 14 per cent. Our unemployment rate six to eight months ago was hovering around the 10 per cent mark. Were other OECD countries doing any better?
The inflation rate in France, in Italy and in the U.K. were running approximately the same or higher than the rate in Canada. In the United States there was roughly the same percentage of unemployment, but, admittedly, it had a better track record in controlling inflation. I suppose we had many alternatives, in terms of economic policy, by way of which to address those issues. Some people in the Opposition were calling for drastic Government program cuts, but they did not
November 30, 1982

wish to specify in which programs they wished to have cuts made. They were calling on others, particularly the Government, to increase the size of the deficit and to stimulate the economy, despite the fact that they knew that would have added to inflationary pressures in Canada which, in turn, would have disastrous effects on productivity and on our ability as a trading nation to export our goods.
Who has the vested interest in high inflation? Who gains by high inflation rates? I would venture to say it is not the elderly who gain by high inflation rates or the poor in our society, who are largely non-unionized and whose wages are unprotected by cost of living arrangements. It is mainly the larger groups in our society, which are protected by cost of living allowances, by union contracts and by their companies, which are protected from the ravages of inflation. I then say to myself, if they are the only ones who gain, how can Hon. Members call the Minister of National Health and Welfare an uncompassionate woman, or say that the Liberal Party does not stand for compassion? If we are to be compassionate in the world, we must ensure that the ones who need protection the most are protected by Government, which is a fundamental requirement. Those people are the ones on fixed incomes, and I would assume that most people over the age of 65 fall into that category. We must also protect those who are non-unionized and the poor.
How will we do that through Bill C-131? In terms of our compassion and the protection shown toward those who are poor, non-unionized and on fixed incomes, I would suggest that it is evidenced by the fact that we have not touched those people on Guaranteed Income Supplements and we have not touched the spouses' allowance by capping the indexation, and these people will be fully protected from inflation. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has moved, along with the Government, to help those who need help the most.
Admittedly, some people over the ages of 65 will share some of the burden of the six and five program. It seems to me that it is a moot point to determine who in Canada will bear the brunt of the six and five program. We can all share in the success of the six and five program. I do not believe there is any reasonable Member of the Opposition who firmly believes that a 10 per cent and 12 per cent world is better than a six and five world. If the economic course of six and five, as set out by the Government, is the best one to follow, then we must all share in it. Admittedly, people receiving Old Age Security will share some of the cost, but I would like to correct some of the information given out by Hon. Members of the Opposition. I am sure it was not done deliberately, but I think that the record has to be correct as to what will be the cost borne by those people over the age of 65.
The Hon. Member from Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) mentioned in her speech that there will be 1.1 million Old Age Security recipients who do not receive Guaranteed Income Supplements and who will lose $290 over the
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
next two years, $70 in 1983 and $220 in 1984, due to the proposed limit on indexation.
My understanding is that the Member for Kingston and the Islands based most of her figures on a release from the National Council of Welfare shortly after the June 28 Budget. The National Council of Welfare assumed an inflation rate of 11 per cent in 1982, 10 per cent in 1983 and 9 per cent in 1984. I am happy to point out to the House that largely as a result of the political direction and the economic direction that we gave in that June 28 Budget to a six and five world, we have in fact had success in the last four to five months. The numbers projected over the years 1983 and 1984 significantly reduce the cost to those Old Age Security recipients. According to recent estimates, the average pensioner receiving Old Age Security will lose only $29 in 1983 and $52 in 1984. That is going to be some reduction to those people-we are not trying to dispute that. Nor are we trying to say that the limit of $8,900 makes that person particularly rich in our society. Where those people on OAS have a vested interest in the six and five program, and I am speaking of those people who only receive OAS, is that large numbers of them have access to some form of a private pension plan that is not indexed. If we are successful in the six and five program in reducing inflation from a 12 per cent and 10 per cent world to a 6 per cent and 5 per cent one, they will make up that money by having the income from their private pension source not subject to such high inflation.
If you are needy, poor, over the age of 65, require the Guaranteed Income Supplement or spouse's allowance there will be no reduction, no capping on the indexation of those programs, and I want to stress that point.
The Member for St. Catharines and a large number of the Members of the Conservative Party pointed out a lot of the wastage in Government programs. It is not only the Opposition who are concerned about wastage in Government programs. We, too, have a vested interest as Members of the Government side. Many times in the House during this last six months either the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has welcomed suggestions by Members of the Opposition in areas and programs in which they feel there is wastage. Both have been willing to investigate those programs and eliminate that wastage where it is required.
I think what we have to realize is that under an Old Age Security system you have to be aware of the size of the program to put this in perspective. I notice that the Member from Elgin mentioned that there was a Cabinet Minister who spent some $177,000 last year in travel across the country. I believe the average person sitting at his home would probably be astounded at that amount of money being spent, but I think in order for us to be effective as the national Government we have to get the message of the Government programs and policies, to all regions of the country, and receive their input. In order to do that we cannot just stay in Ottawa and not go to Vancouver or the Maritimes or the other regions of Quebec and consult with the various groups-

I think the majority of Canadians now realize that all groups in our society are going to have to get behind the Government programs to develop a six and five world. I think if we are realistic and intelligent enough about it, regardless of which Party we represent in this House, we must realize that if we can get inflation rates down to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in this country in the next two years, the social security system will be much stronger in this nation than it is under a 12 per cent or 10 per cent world.
I would hope that in the ensuing debate over the next few days the Members of the Opposition would not give out erroneous statements about the effects of Bill C-131 and not bring in extemporaneous debate on the need for national pension reform, which we have no doubt is required in this country. It is very important that the research people supply correct information on the background for speeches, so we do not have a deluge of letters such as have been received by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and various Members opposite, stating all kinds of untruths with respect to Bill C-131 and the intentions of Government.
This Government is going to win the hearts and the minds of the Canadian people with the six and five program, and the social security system will be that much better for it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I just have one comment for the Liberal Member who just sat down-you have got to be kidding!
We are debating Bill C-131 tonight, which is an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2) and the first reading was on October 28, 1982.
Under the explanatory notes it says here:
Clause 1. New.
This amendment would limit the indexation of the pension to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984.
We all know we have an inflation rate of about 10 per cent. That clearly indicates how senior citizens will fall behind in a very short period under an arrangment like that.
I want to congratulate some of my colleagues in the Conservative Party on the excellent contribution they have made to this debate on the Old Age Security Act and in particular my
colleague, the Hon. Member for Okanagan North (Mr. Dantzer) who, when speaking a couple of days ago on the Bill, stated:
Mr. Speaker, normally I receive a great deal of pleasure in speaking to the various Bills which come into this House, but this afternoon I speak to Bill C-131 with a certain degree of sadness and regret.
All of us on this side of the House support that statement.
Because of this Bill I see the destruction of what I think is a fairly good pension system for Canada. This is certainly a backward step with Bill C-131.
The Member for Okanagan North went on to say:
Our pension system rests on four tiers. We have the Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement which give a basic amount of money to people who retire, we have the Canada Pension Plan which supplements that amount of money for those people in the working force, and we have private pension plans, which are many and varied. Finally, of course, we have personal savings, which include our house and mortgage and RRSPs. This system provides a fairly good pension system in this country.
He goes on to quote statements made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare which supported those pensions, but this Bill certainly takes the steam out of anything she said in the past.
May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INTERNATIONAL INSTITUTE OF APPLIED SYSTEMS ANALYSIS. (B) ATTENDANCE OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS VICE-PRESIDENT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-INTERNATIONAL INSTITUTE OF APPLIED SYSTEMS ANALYSIS. (B) ATTENDANCE OF CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS VICE-PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following my questions concerning Mr. Michael Kirby's attendance at a recent meeting of the International Institute of Applied Systems Analysis held in Austria this month, I received a letter from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Lapierre) noting that the members of IIASA, as it is known in its acronymical form, are "non-Governmental organizations". The letter further states that the United States Government for "primarily budgetary reasons" withdrew its support from IIASA and also that Canada makes an annual contribution to this organization of about $400,000 per year.
Mr. Kirby, according to this same letter, was there as a representative of the Canadian committee. Mr. Kirby apparently is a veritable renaissance man. Like Benvenuto Cellini or Leonardo Da Vinci. This man appears to be an expert on everything: On the Constitution, can anyone forget the famous
November 30, 1982

memorandum; or on the Atlantic fishery, can anyone forget his recommendations there, although some of us would like to; or lately on railways and transportation, since he is now heavily involved in CN as a vice-president? Apparently the man has time left to contribute to the world scientific community. He is truly a remarkable man. Of course, I am not surprised, considering some of his illustrious namesakes, whom we all know. However, I am not fully satisfied with the raison d'etre for us being involved with this particular organization, Mr. Kirby notwithstanding.
First of all, it appears that the withdrawal of the United States from this organization was not for budgetary reasons primarily, as the explanation stated, but rather out of apprehension that a Soviet official who occupied an administrative post at 11 ASA was involved in intelligence activities. An American official was quoted recently in a scientific publication, that the Reagan administration has been concerned that Soviets and Eastern Europe scientists had access to Western data bases through western computers and also that Soviet scientists working at that institute might not be bona fide scientists.
In fairness, this is not an unanimous view in the United States scientific community, but it is significant that the highly respected Royal Society in Great Britain is also getting out of this organization at the end of this year, adding further weight to my contention that our country has better things to do with its money and its bureaucrats than taking part in this organization.
These withdrawals were caused by Soviet abuses of the society's stated aims. The Soviet Union placed into its administration an espionage agent name Arkady Belozerov who was identified by a Norwegian double agent as his Soviet control. Consider as well recent reports from Reuters News Agency which quotes from a United States Senate report. Again I quote:
So dominant a role does American technology place in the Soviet's military and industrial scheme that it is likely that they have come to think of U.S. research and development programs as their own ... Acquisition of American technology has enabled the Kremlin to make giant strides in military strength at a minimum of risk in investment and resources.
This type of information, however, has not impressed one of our federal bureaucrats. Dr. John Stone, a policy advisor in the Department of Science and Technology, who spelled out publicly on behalf of the federal Government that Canada will continue to support the work of the institute, as the criticisms of the institute are hogwash and inspired by new McCarthyites in the Reagan administration. Thirty years after Senator McCarthy, officials and even Ministers in this Government seek to confuse and frustrate legitimate questions on security by this kind of intellectual hogwash.
What troubles me is that the continuing participation by our country, officially or unofficially, in 11 AS A exemplifies our Government's naivete in its dealings with Communist countries.
It accepts all source of dubious characters attached to diplomatic postings here in Canada who come from Eastern
__________________________________21157
Adjournment Debate
Europe, while allowing Warsaw Pact countries, for example, to supply us with their people who may or may not be working in Canada's best interests in those locations where we have embassies and consulates.
We are not at all interested, it would seem, in correcting the situation whereby the Socialist Republic of Czechoslovakia pressures Canadian citizens who have present or former connections with that country, and our Government continues to ignore the passport problems, and tolerates the practice by some Czech-Canadians of travelling to Eastern Europe on Eastern European passports. I know of Public Servants, former Czech citizens, who use Czech passports validated by the Czech Consulate in Montreal on their trips to Czechoslovakia, and use their Canadian passports on the return trips to conceal some of their travel details. We seem to be the leading example among Western countries of Lenin's famous doctrine, "that capitalists will ultimately sell the Communists the very rope that Communists will use to hang them."
I do not think anyone advocates an attitude of complete hostility or paranoia toward Communist countries, but surely we should show a little concern for the area of high technology that the Soviets and their allies are so anxious to obtain from us, in all probability to use against us. We should also, I suggest, have the proper governmental officials speak to people like our Dr. John Stone, who apparently feels free to make remarks of a quite distasteful nature about the administration of President Reagan. I will be watching with great interest to see how IIASA progresses, and I trust that sometime soon we will either achieve some tangible benefits for the world scientific community and, hopefully, for our own country, or we will cease supporting it. Perhaps my hon. friend, when he responds to my questions, will tell me just what benefits we have received so far and how long he thinks we can justify supporting IIASA at a time when we are desperately short of research and development funds in our own country.
I remind the House that one large company in West Germany, for example, the Siemens Company, probably has more resources and more people working in its corporate structure than we have in our entire country, yet we feel quite free to continue to financially support this organization under these conditions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start off by telling my hon. friend that I share his view on the experience and reputation of Mr. Michael Kirby. He is a remarkable man, and that is why I am very proud to see that he has agreed to serve with this institute and participate in its work. We all agree that he is a distin-guised maritimer and he would not participate in any activities which would threaten either the security or reputation of Canada.
We know for a fact that the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis is a multilateral non-governmental

November 30, 1982
Adjournment Debate
research centre, established in 1972 to promote the development and application of systems analysis to the complex management problems facing contemporary society. My hon. friend refers to espionage agents and Soviet abuses. It is very hard for us to understand how an espionage agent could be useful when we know that all IIASA's work is non-confidential and published openly. If the Soviet Union needs an agent to read that stuff, I tell my hon. friend one is not needed, and there is no reason for him to play the Sherlock Holmes game- because in this case this is all public information. Any member of any country can use this material.
In keeping with the nature of the institute, the members are all non-governmental organizations. Canada was a founding member and is represented by the Canadian committee for IIASA. There are 14 other national member organizations from the Soviet Union, the United States, Japan and many European countries. The U.S. government has, according to our information, for primarily budgetary reasons withdrawn its support for IIASA. If the Hon. Member has other facts, we will be happy to check them for him.
Canada's contribution has been $400,000, and it is the responsibility of the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) to decide every year what the contribution will be. The Hon. Member will certainly have the opportunity when the Estimates are brought in to ask questions of the Minister on the relevancy of supplying moneys to this institute. But I want to reassure him that we do not have any worries about any information which could be gathered by some foreign sources. We are proud to say that it is published, nonconfidential and for the use of any country that wants to use it.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-STUDY OF INCOME LEVEL APPLICABLE TO WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE. (B) REQUEST THAT ADJUSTMENTS BE MADE RETROACTIVE
VETERANS AFFAIRS-STUDY OF INCOME LEVEL APPLICABLE TO WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE. (B) REQUEST THAT ADJUSTMENTS BE MADE RETROACTIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pursue in more detail a question I directed to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) on November 19, 1982, dealing with the possibility of raising the casual earnings exemptions for recipients of war veterans allowances, which are presently set at $3,100 for married veterans and $2,100 for single veterans, to a more reasonable level.
The War Veterans Allowance was designed to provide a little extra for veterans who could not claim disabilities under war veterans compensation, and to acknowledge their sacrifices. The War Veterans Allowance Act was brought in 52 years ago. At that time, it was subject to a means test and paid $20 a month for veterans 60 years of age. The Old Age Pension established in 1927 was greatly increased over the years. The means test was removed from the basic pension, and the age was reduced from 70 to 65 years. Yet, the War Veterans Allowance qualifications have remained the same. They have kept the maximum income level at a rate which is certainly unreasonable for 1982. The allowance has changed from being that something extra to being a payment available
for people with incomes below the poverty line. This was not the original intention.
Prime Minister Robert Borden in a speech made to Canadian troops at Vimy Ridge in 1917, stated:
The Government and the country will consider it their first duty to see that a proper appreciation of your effort and of your courage is brought to the notice of your people at home . . . and that no man, whether he goes back or whether he remains in Flanders, will have just cause to reproach the Government for having broken faith with the men who won and the men who died.
This Government has not taken up that duty of showing proper appreciation of our war veterans' efforts of courage. Many of them now reproach their Members of Parliament explaining the unfairness of the present annual allowable income level for War Veterans Allowances. We must realize, and the Government obviously does not, that a person who works for 30 or 40 years deserves his share of the national wealth and productivity. Our veterans are now older and should be justly rewarded for their years of service to this country. Many, being between the ages of 18 and 24, gave the best years of their lives in service for our country.
I approached the Minister of Veterans Affairs on the issue of annual allowable incomes on two separate occasions. On July 15, 1982, the Minister agreed that the annual allowable income for veterans receiving War Veterans Allowances was too low and he promised that steps would be taken to correct the situation. When asked what the new limit would be and when the new amendments would be made, the Minister replied that he was studying the possibility of raising the casual earnings exemption for recipients. He assured me that he was hopeful new legislation would be introduced by the fall of 1982.
On November 19, Mr. Speaker, I questioned the Minister on the present status of his study and when legislation would be passed concerning the annual allowable income for war veterans. The Minister then stated, or rather he enlightened me, that legislation does not have to be passed on this issue; rather an adjustment can be made through the War Veterans Allowance Board. If indeed it is simply an adjustment that needs to be made, why has action not been taken? In the name of all of our war veterans, what is the Minister of Veterans Affairs waiting for? Fall has passed and winter is here, and we have not as yet heard any results from the alleged study. I feel very strongly that the veterans have waited long enough, Mr. Speaker, and I would urge the Minister of Veterans Affairs to give this matter a priority status and report to the House without further delay.

I am somewhat taken aback by the excessive comments which would seem to indicate that the policies of the Government have been less than adequate in terms of its concern and commitment to the wellbeing of our veterans, the non-partisan attitude I have found in committee and to our approaches to make sure our veterans receive the best there is.

Member's question of November 19, 1982, respecting casual earnings exemptions for recipients of War Veterans Allowance, the Minister indicated in the House that the casual earnings levels were last adjusted in July, 1980. The Hon. Member also asked the Minister for some assurance that if the legislation was brought forth after 1982, it would refer back and include 1982. As has already been brought to the attention of the Hon. Member, War Veterans Allowance continues to be fully indexed on a quarterly basis.

In this regard the Chairman advised the Minister that the proposed amendments are based upon the most current information available.

PIPELINES-PROPOSED WATER PIPELINE FROM LAKE DIEFENBAKER TO REGINA, SASKATCHEWAN. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 2, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what progress had been made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) in his discussions with the Province of Saskatchewan, particularly with regard to a proposal to build a pipeline from Lake Diefenbaker to Buffalo Pound. Such a pipeline could supply Regina and Moose Jaw with a much needed supply of fresh, clean water.
This project became a major topic of discussion during the fall municipal elections in Regina. All major candidates running for aldermen and for the position of mayor supported it. In fact, the City of Regina committed itself to support the pipeline financially. There is an arrangement between the workers of Ipsco and the management of the plant to back the idea of a pipeline. They have formed a committee in Regina, the Good Clean Water Committee. In fact, it is an example of labour and management in co-operation. The company is willing to sell the pipe at cost. Approximately 600 jobs will be created in the manufacturing of the pipe and some 570 jobs will be created laying it. It is a project for which there is a tremendous need. Obviously now is the time to build the pipeline.
Adjournment Debate
The response of the Prime Minister to my question was to say the least somewhat flippant. The need for a source of fresh water has been growing in the City of Regina and in fact in the City of Moose Jaw for a number of years. As the City of Regina in particular has grown, so has the need for new, clean, fresh water grown.
A study was commissioned jointly by the City of Regina, the Province of Saskatchewan and I believe the City of Moose Jaw at the beginning of 1981. That committee reported some 14 months later. It recommended that the new source of fresh water for the Moose Jaw and Regina area be delivered and that such a project be undertaken. During the election, the New Democratic Party of Saskatchewan committed itself to bringing a new source of fresh water to Regina and Moose Jaw during the next four years.
The reason the project should proceed now is that over 1,000 steelworkers have been laid off at the Ipsco plant. Large public projects such as the pipeline from Lake Diefenbaker to the Buffalo Pound should be undertaken in periods when there is high unemployment. Therefore, the time to undertake the project is now.
When the Prime Minister responded to my supplementary question, obviously he was not aware that Ipsco had never experienced such a massive lay-off of its workers until the Tories became the Government in Saskatchewan. That makes the difference and it is the reason the project should be undertaken, because of the large number of unemployed workers. This is a way by which these workers could be put back to work. Rather than having them take home unemployment insurance payments, they could be earning real wages. They could be productive and produce pipe needed for this project. Therefore, I was somewhat dismayed at the flippant remarks by the Prime Minister. I hope the Government will take this opportunity tonight to indicate whether it has had further discussions with representatives of the Province of Saskatchewan and whether we can expect an announcement before Christmas that this project will proceed, so that the workers at IPSCO will have some assurance that there will be some work for them at least in the New Year.

subtopic: PIPELINES-PROPOSED WATER PIPELINE FROM LAKE DIEFENBAKER TO REGINA, SASKATCHEWAN. (B) REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a proposal was indeed put forward last summer to the Saskatchewan Government by the Regina based company Ipsco to construct a pipeline from Lake Diefenbaker to Regina and Moose Jaw to provide fresh water to these two areas. The proposed 90 to 100 mile pipeline would not only provide fresh water to the municipalities, but could provide employment for Ipsco workers who have been laid off, or who may face lay-off if conditions in the economy do not improve.
The Saskatchewan Government has received the proposal and established a one-man task force to look into provincial water problems. A report was to have been submitted to the

November 30, 1982
Adjournment Debate
provincial Government in November, but the deadline has been extended until the first week of December. Recommendations on the pipeline can be expected from the task force. Our understanding, Mr. Speaker, is that the Saskatchewan Government will review the recommendations brought forward in the task force report and then decide on options for solutions.
In the meantime, federal Government support has been given to the task force by providing the technical expertise of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Agency. The PFRA will advise the task force on water development needs and potential in Saskatchewan. Since the federal Government has not yet been officially approached by the provincial Government for involvement in the proposed pipeline construction, we have not participated in any discussions with the province. The Government, however, would be willing to consider any recommendations from the Saskatchewan Government that would provide better water, as well as increased employment opportunities to that area.
As Hon. Members know, the federal Government has recently signed an agreement with the Saskatchewan Government to increase employment in that province. The New Employment Expansion and Development Agreement will
provide $15 million for employment in Saskatchewan. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), who is also Chairman of the Western Affairs Committee of Cabinet, has noted the co-operative nature of the negotiations on the NEED Program. Water and soil conservation in the Prairie has been examined as a priority issue by Members of the Western Affairs Committee. We will thus be open to recommendations from the province concerning the pipeline initiative.
